summary: The assessee is a Hindu Undivided Family. In the assessment year 1965 66, the Wealth Tax Officer included in the net wealth of an assessee on the valuation date, the value of the assets and debts of the assessee on that date. The Wealth Tax officer included the amount of Rs. 1, 50, 000 representing the accrued interest on the capital of the company as well as the balance of the amount payable by the assessee to the Revenue. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 3 (1) of the Wealth tax Act, 1957, but he did not accept the contention of the Revenue that the amount paid by the asses se to the assessee should be taken into account for determining the net income of the asses ee. The Tribunal upheld the view of the Income Tax Officer. On appeal, the High Court held that since the assessee had been assessed to wealth tax under the Wealth (1)( 2) of s. 7 of the Act, it was not necessary to determine the net assets of the assesses on the basis of which the net Wealth Tax could be determined. It further held that if the assessee's claim for exemption from wealth tax was accepted, the net asset would have to be valued at the market value of such assets. The High Court also held that there was no justification for the Tribunal to hold that the net worth of the appellant was not less than the net value of all the assets of his wife and that the same was liable to be included in his net wealth. The question referred to the High court was answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave, the question for determination was whether the assessee is entitled to deduction of the net tax of the sum of Rs 1, 00, 000 received by him as a result of the sale of the property in his name. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The assessee has been assessed on the net estate of the deceased. The net wealth is the total wealth of the family. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 of that Act. [ 310 E ] 2. The expression " net wealth " is defined in section 2 (m) of that section to mean the aggregate value of every asset which is capable of being sold or disposed of in any manner including the proceeds of sale. The word " net " is not defined in the Act. The definition of " net assets " in section 4 (1), therefore, includes the net net wealth as defined in clause (m). [ 310 F ] 3. The true scope of the expression " gross wealth " in the context of the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 is that the value must be determined in accordance with the provisions contained in the Income tax Act. If the value is not determined according to the principles laid down in the said Act, the valuation of the asset will be made on the assumption that the asset has been sold or otherwise disposed of. [ 311 A B ] 4. The words " net worth " in sub section 2 of section 6 of the Gift Tax Act are wide enough to include the net profits of the business. The value of a property is not to be determined by reference to the value thereof. The valuation of a particular asset is a matter of inference to be drawn from the facts and circumstances of each case. But where the asset in question is an int angible asset, the cost of acquisition of the same cannot be deducted from the net profit of the owner. [ 312 C D ] 5. The fact that the assets are in the nature of fixed assets does not make them a part of the value. The asset is not merely a fixed asset but is a tangible asset.

The respondent was a public servant. He was dismissed from service by the appellant on the ground that he had been convicted in a criminal case and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of two years. The respondent filed an appeal before the Tribunal which was allowed. The Tribunal held that the respondent was not guilty of any misconduct and, therefore, the order of dismissal was not justified. In the writ petition filed by the respondent, the High Court set aside the order passed by the Tribunal and directed reinstatement of the respondent with back wages. The State Government appealed against the said order. The High Court held that since the respondent had been acquitted in the criminal case, it was not open to the State Government to proceed against him under section 29 of the Act. It further held that there was no evidence to show that the charge framed against the respondent did not warrant his dismissal. The Union of India preferred an appeal to this Court. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of the Tribunal to interfere with the disciplinary proceedings is limited. The scope of interference by the High Courts in the departmental proceedings is very limited. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The jurisdiction of the High court in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the disciplinary authority or the appellate authority is confined only to the grounds on which such finding is based. The adequacy or sufficiency of evidence or the reliability of the evidence cannot be gone into by the Court unless the findings are perverse or the punishment imposed is shocking ly disproportionate to the nature of the charges proved. [ 11 E F ] 3. The expression " any other sufficient reason " used in the rule must mean " good and sufficient reasons ". If the conclusion is based on no evidence, the Tribunal would have no jurisdiction to interfere. [ 12 C ] 4. The word'sufficient'has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary (5th Edn.) as " the equivalent of'not less than one's worth '. This is what is meant by the expression " sufficient cause ". The expression'sufficient cause'means something more than mere inaction or negligence. It does not mean'carelessness '. The word " sufficient " is generally understood to mean'not sufficient cause '. In the context of the rules of natural justice, the expression'has to be given a meaning which it has been used in a particular statute. The question whether the delinquent officer has been able to prove the charge against him or not will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 13 D ] 5. The term " sufficient reason ", in the context, means " adequate and sufficient " and not merely a vague or fan ci ful explanation of the delay in serving the charge sheet. The requirement of the rule is that the delinquent should have been afforded a reasonable opportunity to defend himself. The enquiry report is not a mere formality but a solemn statement of the facts of the case. The disciplinary authority is required to consider the same. The Enquiry Officer is expected to arrive at a definite conclusion. The Disciplinary Authority is also required to take into consideration the representation made by the delinquent employee. The delinquent employee is entitled to know the circumstances in which the allegations were made against him. The record of the enquiry is not necessary to be produced before the disciplinary authorities. The inquiry is not to be conducted by the Enquiry Officer. The Inquiry Officer is not supposed to act as a disciplinary authority. The Inqu iring Authority is not bound to furnish the report of the Enquiry officer. The Presenting Officer is also not required to submit the report to the disciplinary Authority. The report is only an opinion and not the opinion of the disciplinary au tho r ity. The conclusion of the Inquiry Officer on the basis of the report is a tentative one. The findings of the Inqu iring Officer are not final.

The appellant, a tenant of the land in question, filed an application under section 9 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as'the Act ') for possession of the suit property on the ground that he was the lawful tenant of a portion of the said land. The Trial Court dismissed the application holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his title to the suit land and that the defendant No. 1 was not entitled to any relief. In appeal before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been instituted after the expiry of three years from the date of dispossession and that since the suit is within time, the provisions of section 8 (2) of the Act were applicable and the suit should have been decreed. The High Court held that the trial court had jurisdiction to decide the issue whether the suit filed by the appellant was barred under section 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure or not. It further held that even if the suit could be decided on merits, the suit would still be barred by the law of limitation. On this basis, the High court set aside the order of the Trial Court and remanded the matter to the Trial court for deciding the issue afresh. The appellant has challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Courts. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 Section 8 (1)( b) of The Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939 provides that where a person is a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Tenancy Act and such landlord has acquired the right to continue in possession of such land, the Mamlatdar shall, subject to the provisions contained in sections 5 and 6, determine the rent payable by him in respect of the lands in question. [ 10 B ] 1. 2. The expression " the Mamlatdar " used in section 8 is not defined in the Act but it is defined in section 2 (c) of that Act which means the Mamlatdar appointed under the Act. Therefore, the word " Mamlatdar " occurring in section 3 (1) of Act will include the Mamlatdar who is the Collector of the area. [ 11 C D ] 1: 2. 1. The words " the Collector " in section 4 (1), are wide enough to cover the case of a landlord who is a trespasser and who has been evicted from the land on the grounds mentioned in section 7 (1). [ 11 E F ] 1 2. 2 The expression'the Mamlatdar'in section 5 (1)) of the Land Revenue Code is not confined to the Mamlatdar only. The Mamlatdar is not a Mamlatdar. He is a Mamlatdar and the Mamlatdar is the Mamlatdar. The question of the Mamlatdar being a Mamlatdar does not arise. [ 12 G H ] 2. 3. The word'Mamlatdar'is not sy non y mous with the word'Collector '. The word " Collector " is not restricted to the Collector. The Collector is also the Collector and the Collector is the Tahsildar. The Assistant Collector is not the Collector, but the Collector can be the Mamlatdar and therefore the Mamlatdar cannot be the Collector in the present case. [ 13 A ] 2: 2: 3. There is no dispute between the parties that the Collector has the power to decide whether the land is a tenant or not and the same is required to be determined by the Mamlatdar under section 10 of the Abolition Act. [ 14 B ] 2 (i) The word Collector is used in the context of the definition of the word Collector in section 9 (1); the Collector must be the Deputy Collector of a district and the State Government. The State Government is the appropriate Government. [ 15 B ] 3. 1 The word ` Collector'in the definition clause is not limited to the District Collector. But the Collector may be the Commissioner of the Division.

The petitioners are working as car p enters in the Corporation. They were employed by the Corporation as car penter and they were paid a sti pend of Rs. 1, 000 per month. The Corporation has framed a scheme for payment of wages to the employees of the Corporation on the basis of the wage scales applicable to them. The petitioners have been paid a sum of Rs, 2, 500 /- per month as sti pend s. The respondents have not taken any steps to implement the scheme. The petitioner's case is that the work was done by the respondent Corporation in accordance with the terms of the contract between the parties. The respondent Corporation has not taken into account the fact that the petitioners had worked for more than 240 days in a year. The Court has also held that the respondent corporation cannot be directed to pay the minimum wages prescribed under the Act. In the present case, the petitioners have not been able to show that there was any discrimination or arbitrariness in the fixation of the minimum wage. The only ground on which the petitioners claim is that they should be paid at least the minimum rate of wages fixed by the Government. The learned counsel for the petitioners contended that the Corporation has no power to fix the minimum rates of wages and that the same is arbitrary. It is further submitted that the State Government has no authority to fix any minimum wage in respect of the work done by it. The State Government is bound to make the necessary changes in the conditions of service of the workmen. The contention is that since the Corporation is an instrumentality of the State, it is entitled to fix its own minimum wage and that it is not open to the State to discriminate against the petitioners. The second contention is regarding the validity of the provisions of section 3 (b) of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. Section 3 (c) of Act provides that the appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. The relevant part of section 4 of the said Act reads: " 4. (1) Every rule made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agrees that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity or anything previously done under the rule." The petitioners contend that the impugned provision is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it does not provide for the fixing of the maximum wages payable to the workers in the establishment. The argument is that even though the Act does not prescribe the minimum amount of wages but it is provided for the maximum number of the workers to be employed in the establishments in the State. The Act is silent on the question of the fixation and the manner of the payment of the wages. The impugned provision does not indicate that the employer can fix the maximum limit of wages. It merely provides that in the matter of fixing the maximum rate of wage, the maximum wage shall be fixed by reference to the maximum of the scale of wages, the minimum of which is the maximum fixed by law. The object of the impugned legislation is to provide for a minimum wage of Rs 50 per day. The minimum wage is fixed by a statute. The legislature has not provided for any other method of calculation of the amount of the compensation. The Legislature has not enacted the Act in the present form.

The prosecution case against accused 6 and 7 was that on the date of occurrence, he had been in his house at about 1. 30 p. m. when he was sleeping in his room. Accused 5 and 6 were armed with deadly weapons like spe ars, sticks etc. They had also assaulted him with a knife. Accused 6 and 8 were armed and they had also attacked him with kn ives. Accused 2, 3 and 4 were armed. Accused 1 to 4 were having la this. Accused 3 and 5 were armed, while accused 6 was armed with a stick. Accused 4 and 5 had a lathi. Accused 7 and 8 had a sword. Accused 9 and 10 were armed by the same weapon. Accused 11 and 12 were armed along with other accused. Accused 13 and 14 were armed in the same manner as accused 1 to 3. Accused 15 and 16 were armed for the purpose of causing injuries to the deceased. Accused 18 and 19 were armed at the time of the incident. Accused 20 and 21 were armed only with sticks. Accused 22 and 23 were armed armed with sticks and accused 25 was armed. The other accused were armed but they were not armed with any weapons. Accused 24 and 25 were armed on the ground. Accused 26 and 27 were armed when the deceased was being taken to the hospital. Accused 28 and 29 were armed; accused 31 and 32 were armed respectively. Accused 34 and 35 were armed while accused 38 were armed except accused 1 and 2. Accused 37 was armed and accused 38 was armed at that time. Accused 39 was armed, who was armed in a dr un ken state. Accused 40 was armed by a sharp edged weapon. He was armed only when he fired a shot from his gun. Accused 43 was armed when he tried to fire at the deceased with a pistol. Accused 45 was armed but he was not armed. In the course of the occurrence, the accused were seen running away from the place of occurrence. Accused 42 and 44 were armed together. Accused 46 and 48 were armed because they were armed as they were carrying sticks. They were armed to the extent of causing injury to the victim. Accused 47 and 48 had caused injuries to P. W. 1. Accused 52 and others were armed whereas accused 55 were armed which were armed without any weapon. The High Court acquitted all the accused. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, the Court, HELD: (i) The evidence of the eye witnesses is consistent and corroborated by the medical evidence. [ 100 G ] (ii) The presence of the accused at the scene of offence is doubtful. There are no independent witnesses. The evidence regarding the participation of the appellant in the crime is not reliable. [ 101 B ] (iii) The fact that the appellant was armed is not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [ 102 E ] (iv) The conviction of the appellants under section 302 read with section 149 I. P. C. is set aside. [ 103 A ] (v) The High court has rightly convicted the appellant under section 304 Part II I. The sentence awarded to the appellant is reduced to imprisonment for life. [ 104 H ] (vi) The sentence of death imposed upon the appellant by the trial court is confirmed.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in her favour and obtained a decree against her. She also claimed that she had been adopted by her husband's brother, who was the son of one of the daughters of the testator. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether the will is genuine or not has to be determined with reference to the evidence adduced before the court. [ 429 E ] (2) The burden of proof is on the prop ounder to prove the will. It is not necessary that the onus lies on the person who asserts the existence of the will to prove that the will was duly executed. [ 430 A ] (3) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is a rebut table presumption which is rebut table. But the presumption can be rebutted by proof of a fact which is either admitted or proved by the party who asserts it. [ 431 B ] (4) The mere denial of the execution of the document itself is not sufficient to raise a presumption that the signature of the test at rix was that of the leg ate e. [ 432 D ] (5) The onus of proving the will must be discharged by leading cogent and convincing evidence. [ 433 G ] (6) The test at eness of the signatures of the Test at rix is not conclusive. The test is not the usual test of the satisfaction of the court in such cases. [ 434 C ] (7) The court may presume that the attesting witness had signed the will as a witness. If the attesting witnesses were un willing to sign the will, the court would have no difficulty in accepting the will in the absence of any other evidence. The court should not insist upon the production of the Will in order to satisfy its conscience. [ 435 F ] (8) The courts below have failed to appreciate the true import of the provisions of section 68 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. [ 436 H ] (9) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the estate of the last holder of the property.

The appellants are manufacturers of electrical energy. They were paying duty on the goods manufactured by them and cleared from their factory under a valid invoice. The Assistant Collector held that the goods were classifiable under Item No. 4, but he did not accept the contention of the appellants that they were parts of electric power driven pumps. He also held that there was no evidence to show that the appellants had used the said power driven pump for the purpose of manufacture of electric energy. The Appellate Collector held in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " parts " occurring in entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the Act means parts which are capable of being used as parts of motor vehicles or apparatus for the use of the motor vehicle. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: (1) The word " parts ", in its ordinary meaning, is used in the sense of a number of articles which are used for the purposes of the business of the company. It is not possible to hold that the words " parts of the machinery " do not mean that the parts must be used for some other purpose. [ 562 E ] (2) The expression " accessories " is not defined in the Act. The expression'parts'has been defined in section 2 (d) of the Act to mean " parts which have been used for any purpose whatsoever ". The expression includes parts which may be used in connection with the business or profession of the person who carries on the business. The definition of " parts'in the explanation to the definition of the expression'part'in section 3 (b) of that Act makes it clear that the word " accessories'does not include parts which can be used as part of the machine. [ 563 A ] (3) The term " parts '' in the context of the definition in section 4 (1)( a) of Act cannot be construed to mean parts which would be used only for the manufacture of the goods. The word'parts ', in the present case, is not used in a technical sense. The dictionary meaning of the word'accessories'is " parts ". The word is used to describe the items in the commercial sense. It will be noticed that the term " accessories ", in the Dictionary of English Language, is " an article of the same kind or description, that is to say, a piece of metal, or a combination of two or more of these things, that are used in relation to the manufacture or production of the articles." The word ings of the statute are not sy non y mous with the word ings used in section 5 (1). The word, " parts," in the definition, therefore, refers to the articles which may or may not be used, in the process of manufacture. [ 564 C; 565 B ] (4) The words " components " and " parts thereof " in the Explanation to the expression in the notification are not intended to cover the entire article. The words are used to indicate that the article should be used primarily for the production of articles. The use of such articles in the manufacture, of the article itself, is a matter of common knowledge and experience. The fact that the articles are used as component parts of a particular article or article, in its popular sense, is of significance. The question whether the article is a part of a single article or a whole article is not relevant. The test is whether the articles in question are used by the manufacturer in the industry in which the article has been used. If the article in question is not a part and parcel of the whole article, it is not necessary to prove that the item is a component part of that article.

The petitioners are the lessees of minor minerals in respect of which a notification was issued under section 15 (1) of the Act. They were granted mining leases for quarrying stone, gra vel and ordinary cl ay. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notifications on various grounds. It was contended that the State Government had no power to make rules regulating the grant of mining leases or other mineral concessions in respect thereof. The State Government did not have any power to frame rules regulating grant of lease or licence. The Rules framed by the State of Gujarat were ultra vires the powers conferred upon it by section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. The High Court held that the power exercised by the Central Government under section 3 of the aforesaid Act was legislative in character and could not be questioned in view of the provisions contained in section 15. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power of the State Legislature to make a rule is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. [ 409 E ] (ii) The State has the power to legislate with regard to matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule. The power to regulate the grant or renewal of mining lease or other minerals is vested in the State. [ 410 A ] (iii) The word'regulation'in Entry 54 of List II of the VII th Schedule to the Constitution means regulation of mines and mineral development as defined in section 2 (b) of that Act. The expression'regulation of mining'is wide enough to include all matters relating to the grant, renewal or renewal. The word " regulation " in entry 54 of the same list includes the power of making regulations. [ 411 G ] (iv) The words " regulation of the mines and minerals " in Entry 23 of List III of the 7th Schedule to that Act are wide enough and do not exclude the power conferred by the said entry. The words'regulation and development'in entry 23 of the Concurrent List are not sy non y mous with the words " subject to " occurring in entry 52 of List I. The latter entry is an entry relating to " mines and quar ries ". [ 412 C ] (v) The expression " regulation and mining " in the context of entry 54 in List II must be read in the light of the definition of the word " industry " in section 3 (c) of Act. [ 413 B ] (vi) The term " regulation ", in its ordinary meaning, is used in the sense of " regulation ". The word is not a generic one but is a word of broad import. The dictionary meaning of the expression " control over the mines " is " to control the mining operations ". The expression is not only used in entry 24 of List 11 of the seventh schedule to the Indian Constitution, but also includes the powers of the Union and the States to make laws in respect to the matters enumerated therein. The Parliament has enacted the Mines & Minerals (Regulations and Development and Mineral Concession s) Act. 1957. Section 15 of that is a provision which empowers the Central and the State Governments to make regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions thereof. [ 414 F H; 415 A ] The word ings of the section indicate that the word'control'is not merely a word or phrase. The use of the words'in the matter of'or'in'is indicative of the fact that the legislature has made a distinction between the two. The first part of the sub clause (a) of section 3 provides that the Central or the State Legislatures may make rules for regulating the procedure for the exercise of the right conferred by section 3. The second part of section 4 (1)( a) provides that no such rules shall be made after the commencement of the Ordinance unless the State has made such rules.

The appellant was a trustee of the temple of the respondent. He had been appointed as a trustee in the temple and his office was abolished by the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The appellant's appointment was made on the basis that he was a hereditary trustee. The question for consideration is whether the appellant was entitled to succeed to the office of trustee. Held, that the appellant could not be said to have any right to continue as a hereditary manager after the death of the f ounder. The word " succession " in section 6 (9) of the Act must be construed along with the expression " succession to the property ". In the present case the appellant had no right to hold the office. It was only an act of succession which was to be governed by the provisions of the Madras Act. The definition of " hereditary trustee " in the Act would include even a person who has been appointed under the Act. Section 6 (1)( b) of that Act provides that the term " hereditary trustees " means the trustees of a religious institution or a math or other religious institution. The expression " hereditary Trustee " in this context means a person whose name is entered in the register of members of a public trust. The words " hereditary Trustees " in sub section (2) of section 6 are wide enough to include persons who are not merely hereditary trustees but also persons who have been appointed by the Government. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the suit filed by the appellant against the respondents was barred by limitation.

The appellant was tried for the murder of his brother. He was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, which was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in convicting him under section 304 Part II I. P. C. and sentencing him to imprisonment for life. It was also urged that the conviction of the accused under section 201 I. PC was not sustainable because there was no evidence to show that he had any motive to commit the crime. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt. [ 709 E ] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to establish the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubts. [ 710 G ] 3. The evidence of PW 4 is corroborated by the contents of the FIR. There are no reasons to disbelieve the testimony of PW 5. The fact that the deceased was only one among the assailants who was sleeping on a bench outside the house of the deceased does not mean that the accused were guilty of the offence. [ 711 D ] 4. The presence of the two eye witnesses at the scene of occurrence is doubtful. The incident took place at about 10. 30 p. m. and the deceased died at about 11. 15 p. M. The post mortem examination report shows that there were more than one assailant. The deceased was lying unconscious near the door of the house. The accused persons were seen running away from the place of occurrence. The dead body was found at the spot. The inquest report shows the presence of blood stains on the clothes of the victim. The medical evidence shows that the injuries were caused by the accused with the weapon of offence. The doctor who conducted the postmortem examination has stated that the cause of death was due to shock and haemor rhage as a result of ante mortem injury. The injuries were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of Amar chand. They had been assessed to income tax in the hands of the respondents under section 24 B of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessment was made on the basis that the respondents were entitled to be taxed as their legal representatives. The Income tax Officer held that the amount of Rs. 37, 847 / was not liable to be assessed as income of the deceased person but it was a capital receipt which was liable to tax under section 23 (1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. On appeal by the respondents the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. In the second appeal before the Tribunal the question for decision was whether the sum of Rs 37, 848 / was assessable as income from business or as income received by the deceased in the previous year. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the sum received by way of salary was not taxable as income in the earlier years. Held: (i) that the payment of Rs 1, 000 was not an expenditure incurred by the respondent in the course of his employment and therefore the amount could not be said to have been received by him in the subsequent years; (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had paid any money to the deceased at all and that the amounts were not received by them in the past; (iii) that even if the amount was received by a person who is not a resident of the State, the same would be deemed to have accrued to him in that State only when he has actually received the amount and not otherwise. (iv) that in the present case the amount received by one of the appellants was not a capital or revenue receipt and hence the amount must be treated as income. (v) that since the amount in question was received in the year of account of the respondent, the amount should be regarded as having been received in his previous year and not in the current year. (vi) that this amount was not received in any other year and was not in fact received in that year. [ 10 66 E ] (vii) that though the amount had been received as compensation in the first year of the assessment year, the respondent did not receive the amount as such because the amount remained unpaid in the next year. Therefore, the question of the amount being treated as capital receipt does not arise.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State. They were working in the Secretariat of the Andhra State and were posted at Hyderabad. In the year 1958, they were transferred to Hyderabad. On January 19, 1969, they filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 3 of the Act on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of the impugned Act were not discriminatory and that the power conferred by section 3 was not arbitrary or unreasonable. It further held that the impugned order was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power given to the Central Government under section 3 is a legislative power and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily. [ 122 E ] (2) Section 3 of Act No. 21 of 1957 does not confer any power on the Central government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the said Act. The power is given to make Rules for the purposes mentioned therein. The rules are made under the Act. Therefore, the power given by section 4 of the Rules is an enabling provision. [ 123 D ] (3) The words " any requirement " in section 3 do not mean that the rule making authority must have regard to the conditions of service of persons employed in the public services. The word'conditions'in section 4 means'conditions of employment '. The expression'conditions ', therefore, includes conditions of work and conditions of labour. [ 124 A C ] (4) The word " conditions " in the context of section 4 (1)( b) of the A. P. (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1959, means the conditions which are required to be fulfilled before the application of the rule can be granted. [ 125 G ] (5) The expression " conditions of employ ments " in sub section (1), (2), (3), (4), (6) and (7) of section 2 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, clearly indicate that the legislature has used the word " may " in clause (b) and the words " shall " and " shall have the same meaning as " shall ". The word is not defined in the Act but the word'shall'is used in the sense of'shall '. The word used in section 2 (b), (c) and section 2, (d) of Act, makes it clear that the word is used to den ote the condition of the person who is to be appointed to the post. The words'shall be subject to the control of the Governor'in the proviso to section 3 (1). The word ` shall'in clause 2 (a) of Section 2 (1); and the word ` may'in sub sections (2)( a) and 2 (c), respectively, of section 11 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which are relevant for the present case, read as follows: " 2.
