The appellant was a post office and the respondent was in charge of the post office. He was not in possession of any article of the like nature which he had purchased from the appellant. The articles were found in his possession by the police officers who were present at the time when the articles were seized. The appellant's father was also in possession thereof. The High Court held that the appellant had secre ted the articles and therefore, it could not be said that he had secre tered them out of the articles. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the evidence showed that the articles belonged to him and that the prosecution had failed to prove that they belonged to the appellant and that there was no evidence to show that the ornaments belonged to his father. Held, that the presumption under section 114 (g) of the Evidence Act is not available to the accused if the same is rebutted by the evidence of the witnesses. It is only when the court is satisfied that the accused has committed an offence and that he has been guilty of the offence, then the burden is upon him to prove the contrary. The fact that the property belongs to the father does not necessarily mean that the person who claims ownership must have known that the thing belongs to him. The mere fact that he is the owner of the property would not make him a person who is in possession. The burden of proof lies on the person claiming the property to establish that he was in possession and that it was not the person in whose possession the property was. The onus of proving that the possession was with the person entitled to the property is on the party who alleges it. The question whether the person is in exclusive possession or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the person against whom the burden of proving the possession of the thing is placed is examined as a witness, the burden shifts to the person alleging the possession to establish the particular fact. The person who asserts the existence of the fact must be examined as the person to whom the thing belonged. The evidence of a person is not required to be tested by cross examination. But if the person asserting the possession is not examined, the question of his being in possession is irrelevant. The presumption of truth attached to the evidence regarding the possession may be rebutted by other evidence. The persons who are interested in the matter of proof of possession of property and who claim to be in possession are generally interested in seeing that the documents are not tampered with. The Court should not rely on the mere fact of possession in favour of a party unless the person concerned is called upon to produce some evidence in support of his plea. The party seeking to set up a plea of adverse possession must establish that the possess or had the knowledge of the true state of affairs. The plaintiff must further establish that his possession was hostile to the real owner and that his title to the land was hostile. The defendant in his written statement denied the allegation that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. On appeal to the Supreme Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the High court that the plaintiff was in adverse possession of a part of the suit property is based on the evidence adduced by the parties. [ 410 A ] 2. The possession of one of the defendants in the suit is proved beyond doubt. The first appellate court has rightly rejected the evidence led by the plaintiff. The second appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was convicted under section 120 (b) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of two years. He filed an application before the High Court for stay of the proceedings in the High court. The High Court dismissed his application on the ground that he had not been able to prove that the order of the High, Court was not served upon him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the appellant had knowledge of the order passed by the High Magistrate and that the conviction was bad because the High. Court did not consider the question whether the order was served on the appellant or not. Held: (i) The High Courts have power to issue writs under article 226 of the Constitution against any person or authority including the Government. The power conferred on the High courts under article 227 is a very wide power. It must be exercised sparingly and only in appropriate cases. There can be no doubt that the power conferred by article 227 cannot be exercised so as to null ify the orders of the subordinate courts. The powers conferred on them are wide enough to enable them to do substantial justice between the parties. The jurisdiction conferred on these authorities is a judicial power and they should be exercised within the limits of their authority. The Court has no power to interfere with the exercise of such power. The decision of the Supreme Court in the case of State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, [ 1952 ] S. C. R. 284, relied on. (ii) The power of the Court to quash criminal proceedings is a serious matter and the Court should not lightly interfere with an order of acquittal unless there is some manifest error apparent on the face of the record. The revisional jurisdiction of the court should not be exercised to correct errors of law or fact which may have crept in the judgment of the lower court. (iii) The inherent powers of the superior courts are not to be exercised in the light of the facts of each case. But it is equally well settled that the powers possessed by the inferior courts are very wide and the court would be justified in interfering with the order if it appears to be perverse or based on no evidence or on irrelevant considerations or on a consideration of irrelevant considerations. The court will not act like a court of appeal and substitute its own opinion for that of the inferior court. In the present case the High'Court was right in taking the view that the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. The order of remand was made by the Sessions judge after hearing both sides and after considering the evidence and the documents produced by the prosecution. The Sessions Judge was therefore justified in refusing to take cognizance of the offence. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the trial court had given a finding that the accused had committed the offence punishable under section 302 I. P. C., but the High C ould not have taken the view of the Sessions Court that the offence was not proved beyond all reasonable doubt. The contention of the learned counsel is that the Magistrate had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence adduced by the complainant and the witnesses examined by the police and the Magistrate and the High Cour t was not at all relevant to the case. The Magistrate had also not considered the evidence of the witnesses who were examined by him. The evidence of these witnesses was not considered by the Magistrate. The Additional Sessions Judge held that the evidence was sufficient to prove the charge against the accused and acquitted the accused. The revision petition filed by the State of U. P., was allowed and the order dated December 20, 1963 was set aside. The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed to this court. HELD: (1) The order passed in the present proceedings was not a final order.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, I. P. C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. He appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence of Uj agar Singh was not sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and that the High court erred in accepting the evidence regarding the motive of the crime. Held: (1) that the prosecution had failed to prove the motive for the murder of Sheo Sahai and that there was no direct evidence to show that the appellant had committed the murder. (2) that there were circumstances which showed that the deceased was murdered at the time when he was killed and that he had been falsely implicated in the case. (3) that as the appellant's conduct was unnatural, he must have known that the murder was committed by him. (4) that he was a person who had no enmity with the appellant and that if he had any motive to kill him, he would have done so because he was an old man and could not be expected to know what happened to him. It is true that the fact that the accused was a young man of 20 years would not make him a reliable witness. But where the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubts, the question of motive does not arise. The mere fact that a person is a member of the family of the deceased does not necessarily mean that he is a person of unsound mind. The fact that he has been living separately from the deceased or that he may have been living with his wife or that she was married to the appellant does not lead to the inference that the said circumstance was not a circumstance which would justify the conclusion that the offence was committed. The only circumstance relied upon by the prosecution was that the house of the appellants was situated in a busy locality and that they had been living in the same locality. There was no reason why the house should have been situated in the neighbourhood of the village. The house of one of the brothers of the other was situated near the house. The appellant'was a resident of the same village and was residing in the adjoining village. If the house was situated at a distance of about half a mile from the house, the appellant would have been sleeping in the house and would have gone to the house to see the house in the night. The evidence of the two witnesses shows that the houses of the three brothers were situated in close proximity to each other. The first information report lodged by the appellant was recorded by the police officer in the presence of the Sub Inspector of Police and the second. The third witness, who was examined by the defence, stated that the place of occurrence was a little away from the village and that it was a dark night. This statement was made before the police and the police station. The police station was about 10 mil es away from where the dead body of the victim was recovered. The investigating officer did not find any blood stains on the clothes of the victims. The Investigating Officer also did not take any blood stained earth from the scene of occurrence. The trial court and the High, Court found that the recovery of the blood stained clothes of both the victims was doubtful. The learned Judges of the High Courts held that the discovery of the clothes and the clothes contained human blood. The blood group of the dead bodies of the four persons who were present at the spot, the blood stains of the shirt worn by the deceased and the blood group ing of the body of deceased and blood stained soil and the knife used in the commission of the offence. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused. The State of U. P., filed an appeal to the Supreme Court.

The petitioners, who were elected as members of the Municipal Corporation of Raipur, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the election of the respondent No. 1 on the ground that he was not qualified to be chosen to fill the seat reserved for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had failed to establish his case that he had been duly nominated by the Returning Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in law in holding that there was no material before the Returning officer to show that the nomination paper of the appellant was improperly rejected. It was further contended that the Returning Officers had not given any reason why they should have rejected the nomination papers of the candidates. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: (i) The High court has rightly held that the rejection of the nomination of the candidate was improper. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) The order passed by the High, Court is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the High. Court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. [ 11 32 C ] (iii) The question whether the Returning officers had made any mistake in the nomination or not is a matter which can be decided only after the scrutiny of the nominations. [ 12 35 E ] (iv) The Returning Officer had not taken into account the fact that the names of the successful candidates were not included in the electoral roll. The Returning Officers could not have accepted the nomination forms without giving them an opportunity to explain their position. [ 13 36 A ] (v) The Election Tribunal was justified in rejecting the nomination. [ 37 D ] (vi) The decision of the High Courts in regard to the validity or otherwise of the Returning Office's decision cannot be sustained. [ 38 G ] (vii) The election of a returned candidate must be set aside if the result of the elections is not materially affected. [ 39 F ] (viii) The expression " shall be read as " may be substituted for " used in the proviso to sub section (2) of Section 33 of the Act. [ 40 H;

The appellant company was a public limited company. It had been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn, cotton yarn etc., in the State of Bombay. The appellant's company was prosecuted for breach es of sections 32 and 131 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The High Court held that section 134 (4) did not apply to the case because it was not a case where an accused person could be said to have committed any offence under section 132 (1). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 133 (3) is a composite one which provides for the prosecution of persons who are liable to be punished under section 135. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) The expression " any person " in section 133 (1) means a person who is liable to punishment under section 134. [ 11 31 C ] (iii) The word " person " has not been defined in the Code. The word'person'is used in the sense of a person or body of persons. A person may be a company or a firm or a company. But there is no definition of the word " company ". The word is used as a verb. The words " any company " do not mean a jur istic person. The term " person ", therefore, must be given its ordinary meaning. [ 12 31 D ] (iv) The words'any person'in section 132 are wide enough to include a company and a firm. The expression'person ', in the context of section 132, does not mean only a jur id ical person but includes a company, a firm, a company as well as a firm and a company in the same sense. [ 13 31 E ] (v) The use of the expression " person'does not necessarily mean a person other than a company; it is not necessary that the person should be a jur al person. [ 14 31 G ] (vi) The section does not say that the word'company'means a jur ist. It is a jur ical person. It does not refer to a jur isd ic person. There is no reason why the word is not used in section 134 of the Act. [ 15 31 F ] (vii) The question whether the word ` person'occurring in section 131 (2) of the Companies Act is a person's own or a jur ists'or a person is a company is a question of fact. [ 16 31 H ] (viii) The provisions of section 133 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 are not applicable to the present case. [ 17 31 C ]. (ix) The appellant is a private limited company and the directors of the company are not liable to pay tax under section 133. [ 18 31 C, 19 A ] (x) The contention that the appellant is not a jur y person cannot be accepted. The section is not intended to cover a company like the appellant. The company is not an individual. The directors of a company can be treated as a company if they are distinct entities. The companies are different from the company. The shareholders of the appellant company are different. The Directors of the Company are different persons. The director ate of the companies is different from each other.

The appellant was convicted under section 5 (1) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a term of three years. He was also convicted under sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act and sentenced by the Special Judge to undergo rigorous imprisonment of six months. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 5 of Act XX III of 1950 were not applicable to the case because the Act did not apply to the present case as the Act had been repealed by the Act. Held: (i) that the Act was not applicable in the present instance; (ii) that there was no provision in the Act which made the Act applicable to cases where the Act applied to the facts of the present cases; (iii) that section 5 was inapplicable to the cases where there was an express provision in section 5 itself for the application of the provisions contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure to the proceedings before the Special Court. The Act was therefore not applicable. (iv) that even if the Act is not applicable, the provisions thereof would be applicable to all cases irrespective of whether they are pending or not. (v) that in any event the provisions in the [ Code of Civil Procedure ] relating to appeals from original decrees should be construed in accordance with the provisions laid down in the code of Civil procedure and the rules framed thereunder. (vi) that since the Act does not apply, the Act applies to the trial of the cases referred to in the said sub section. (vii) that Section 5 of Ordinance No. 2 of 1949 was not attracted. (viii) that as the provisions were not made applicable to those cases, the question of applicability of the said provisions did not arise.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service on a permanent basis. He was given a pay scale of Rs. 300 - 600 and he was also entitled to be promoted to the post of Professor of Radi ology, which is equivalent to the pay scale attached to the said post. The appellant's claim for promotion to the higher post of Associate Professor was rejected by the Government of India on the ground that it was not a case of promotion but only a temporary measure. The High Court held that the appellant had acquired the requisite qualification for being considered for appointment to the posts of Professor in Orth opaed ics and that his services were liable to be terminated at any time without notice or assigning any reason. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant has been working as a Research Officer in the Department of Orth opaed ic and General Medicine and has been discharging the duties of a Professor of Orth oped ics and a Lecturer in Orth oped ic Surgery. [ 80 E ] (2) The post of Assistant Professor in a Medical College is a teaching post and the appellant is an employee of the Institute. It is not a post carrying a pay - scale of pay. The post carries a pay band and the post carries the same pay scale. The nature of work assigned to the appellant does not change with the post. [ 81 G ] (3) The fact that the post is a non teaching post cannot affect the validity of the order passed by the State Government. [ 82 A ] (4) The question whether the post in question is a post under the Central Government or not is a matter for the State to decide. [ 83 B ] (5) The decision of the Government is final and conclusive. [ 84 C ] (6) The expression " post " used in r. 8 (2A) means a post in the cadre of the Central or State Government or a post borne on the cadre. The word " post ", therefore, must be understood in the context of the rules of recruitment made by the Central Govt. and the State Governments. [ 85 D ] (7) The words " post in a cadre " in the rule are wide enough to include all posts in the service. The expression'post'in the rules would mean a post included in the Cadre of the Indian Administrative Service. [ 86 H;

The workmen of the Company, who were working in different industries, had been awarded bonus at the rate of Rs. 84 per month and the workmen had been paid a minimum wage of Rs, 100 per month. In the case of the workmen, the Tribunal found that there was no comparable work for them and therefore, it was not possible to fix the minimum wage at Rs. 85 per month as against the minimum wages fixed by the Tribunal. The Tribunal also held that the workmen were entitled to receive only one half of the minimum basic wage and dearness allowance on the basis of the total wages paid to them. The workmen appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the minimum monthly wage should be taken into account while fixing the minimum rate of wages. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding in favour of the appellants that the maximum wage which the workmen would get under the Award must be taken to be the minimum of the scale of pay prescribed by the award. [ 10 B ] (2) The fact that the wage structure of the company is being revised from time to time cannot be a ground for denying the benefit of the award to the workmen. [ 11 C D ] (3) The question whether the wage scales are to be revised or not has to be decided on the facts of each case. If the wage scale is revised, the wage - structure will have to be re fixed. The wage structure may be changed if the wage revision is made applicable to all the employees. But the wage fixation can be done only after taking into consideration the wage drawn by the workmen and other relevant factors. [ 12 E F ] (4) The concept of " wage structure " is not an abstract doctrine but is a principle evolved by courts to give effect to the concept of wage structure. [ 13 G ] (5) The principle of " equal pay for equal work " is a face t of the rule of law and is based on the principle of equal pay. There is no difference between the principle laid down in the present case and the principle enunciated in the earlier cases. [ 14 H; 15 A ] (6) The decision in the case was rendered on the footing that the workers were entitled for the same wages as the workmen in the instant case. [ 16 C ] (7) The contention that the principle contained in the judgment of the High Court was not correct in view of the fact that in the matter of payment of bonus, the workmen are entitled to the same remuneration as the permanent workmen and they are entitled for such wages as are given in the award of the Labour Court.

The appellant company was assessed to tax for the assessment year 1960 61. In the assessment proceedings, it was alleged that the Income Tax Officer had failed to make a proper enquiry and had not given any notice under section 148 of the Act. The Income Tax officer issued a notice under sections 148 and 151 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 on the ground that the assessee had concealed the material facts from the Income tax Officer. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the order of the Income - tax Officer was erroneous and set aside the order passed by the Income T ax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for the relevant assessment years. It also held that in view of the fact that the appellant had not disclosed all the material particulars, the Income'tax Officer could not have issued a fresh notice under Section 148. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the notice under s. 148 was invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 149 (2) of the 1961 Act. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 147 are mandatory and must be complied with. [ 446 G ] 2. The words " reason to believe " used in section 147 (a) of Income Tax, 1961 are of wide import. They are not sy non y mous with the expression " reason " or " reasons to believe ". The word " reason ", which is used in the statute, has been used in its wid est sense. The word'reason'means something more than mere pre t ence. It cannot be construed in a narrow way. It has a wider connotation. It includes not only the act done by the assessee himself but also by his agent. The expression " reasons " does not mean " reasons for the belief ". [ 447 B ] 3. The power conferred upon the Income, Tax Officer under section 147 is a very wide one. It is not intended to be used as a sh ield or a tool to circum vent the statutory provision. It can be invoked only when the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer is based on some material which is not germane to the issue. The satisfaction of such a belief is not a condition precedent for the exercise of the power. [ 448 E ] 4. The object of section 148 is to prevent evasion of tax. The section provides that if the Income is found to be insufficient, the Assessing Authority may serve on the person concerned a notice requiring him to furnish a return of his total income. If he fails to do so, the notice would be invalid. [ 449 C ] 5. The language of section 150 (2)( b) is clear and unambiguous. There is nothing in the language of the section which requires that the Assessing authority should record reasons for issuing the notice. The requirement of the law is that the person making the return must be given an opportunity to explain his case. The notice is required to be served on the assessee. The Assessing Officer has to give the assessee a reasonable opportunity to meet the case. He has to satisfy himself that the return is correct and complete. [ 450 A ] 6. The question whether the Income was properly computed and the assessment made in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Act is a matter of fact. The assessee has not been able to produce any evidence to prove that the returns were incorrect. The burden of proof is on the Revenue. [ 451 D ] 7. The failure to furnish the return of income is a valid ground for the purpose of section 34 (1) of 1922 Act. [ 452 F ] 8.

The appellant firm was a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M / s. J es ing bhai Uj am shi & Co., Bombay, which had been registered as a limited company under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The firm was dissolved by a deed of dissolution dated October 30, 1943. The appellant's case was that the firm was not liable to be taxed under section 25 (4) of the Indian In com et ax Act, 19 18, because it was a joint Hindu family and its income from the business carried on by it was exempt from tax under section 26 (2). The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption on the ground that the assessee had no right to carry on business as a partner in the firm. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the partnership was a separate legal entity and that the partners were entitled to the benefit of section 25 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word " firm " in section 25 is wide enough to include a firm in which there are more than one partners. It was further urged that the words " firm in respect of which the firm is constituted " in the definition of " firm ", in section 2 (1)( c) of that Act, must mean a firm which has been carrying on the business of selling goods or supplying goods. HELD: (i) The expression " firm'in section 3 (b) of Act of 19 18 means a firm of which any person is a partner. [ 10 B ] (ii) The word " Firm " in clause (c) does not refer to a firm but only to a partnership. The word'firm'is defined in section 5 (6) of which reads as follows: " A firm shall be deemed to have been constituted for the purpose of this Act, if the persons who have signed the application for registration under this Act are different persons." The word firm is defined by section 2 of the said Act as meaning a firm consisting of two or more persons. The first part of the definition is an inclusive definition and the second part refers to a company. The definition of the word'company'in the Companies Act includes a company incorporated under the Companies Acts. The second part of section 2 defines a firm as a firm whose principal place of business is the place where the business is carried on. The third part of that definition is intended to cover a firm, which carries on the same business as the other firms. The question is whether the word firm in section 24 (2) of this statute can be construed in the light of the provisions of the Income Tax Act. Section 25 (2)( a) provides that the profits of a firm shall, for the purposes of the business, be computed in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act, and the total income of the previous year of the firm as reduced by the amount of income - tax payable under the Act and the income of each of the three years immediately preceding the assessment year. The relevant portion of section 24 is extracted below: " The following classes of cases may be referred to the High Court for its decision, namely:- (1) Where the assessee is a firm the firm in the hands of the partners of the deceased person; (2), where the firm has been dissolved, the firm shall have all the assets and liabilities of the partnership; (3) where the assessee has been assessed to tax and the tax due from him has been paid by the firm, the tax shall be payable by the assessee according to the provisions relating to the firm; (4).

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the deceased, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of her share in the joint family properties. She claimed that she was entitled to a 7 / 24th share in all the properties which were allotted to her husband by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The trial court held that the property belonged to the joint Hindu family and that the plaintiff had no right to claim any share in it. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by special leave, the question is whether the property belonging to the appellant's father was his self acquired property or not. It is true that the appellant has been able to establish that he was entitled only to 1 / 4th share in his own property as his son. But the fact remains that the entire property was purchased by him from his father's brother who died on June 27, 1960. The appellant'S case is that the said property was ancestral property and that there was no partition between him and his two sons. The High Court has also found that the properties were ancestral property. The finding of the High court that the suit property was not ancestral property is correct. The question is: whether the appellant could be treated as having acquired an absolute title by adverse possession ? The High court has taken the view that the sale deed executed by the appellant in favour of his wife was invalid because the same was not supported by consideration. The contention of the appellant is that since the property was sold to his wife by her husband, the property devol ved upon his wife and the daughter, the appellant being the adopted son of the first respondent. The second contention of Mr. N. C. Chatterjee, learned counsel for the appellant, is that even if the property is ancestral property, the same cannot be partitioned. He relied on the decision of the Bombay High Court in Ram krishna vs Bal krishna (A. I. R. 1943 Bom. 128) where the High Courts have held that when the property belongs to the wife of the husband, it is not necessary to go into the question of the nature of the property. In support of this proposition, reliance was placed on the observations made by the Privy Council in the case of [ H. M. S. V. Raja & Ors. vs Mst. Bibi Haz ra & Ors.]; and the decision in the present case of the Madras High Court reported in AIR 19 18 Mad. 10 46. The learned counsel appearing for the respondents contended that the decision does not lay down the correct law and the ratio of the decision is not applicable to the facts of the present appeal. The decision of this Court in the above mentioned cases is not relevant to the present controversy. The point raised before us is that in the instant case, the parties are governed by the Mit aksh ara Law and the principles of Hindu Law are not applicable. The decisions cited by the learned counsel do not help the appellant. The principle of Hindu law is well settled that the rule of construction of will's is based on the maxim " expres sio uni us est exclu sio alter i us ". The rule of interpretation is that where the words of a statute are clear and unambiguous, they must be given their plain meaning. This rule is based upon the maxim'expres sio. ut res ip sa es se non po test ament ary u pr ight am o unt, which means " the law is fairly well settled." The rule is that when a word is used in a statute, it must be construed according to the language employed therein, and the subject matter with regard to which it is used is not the same as the law in general.

The appellant Corporation was established in the year 1956. It was a body corporate under the [ Indian Companies Act, 1913 ]. Under section 3 of the said Act, it was empowered to make regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 4 (1) of the Employees'State Insurance Act, 1948, the Central Government framed the Employees State Insurance (General) Regulations, 1960. Regulation 19 (2) provided that the employees of the Corporation shall be governed by the same conditions as are applicable to other employees of similar status in the establishment. Regulation 20 (2)( b) provided for the constitution of the Board of Directors of the Company. Clause (c) of sub regulation (2), which is relevant for the present case, provides that the Board may appoint such number of officers and other employees as it thinks fit to be the members of the staff of the company. Clause 5 (d) of Regulation 20 provides that every employee of the corporation shall be entitled to receive from the Corporation an ann uity equivalent to the amount of his pay and allowances for each completed year of service or part thereof, whichever is less. The appellant was appointed on January 30, 1955. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer with effect from April 1, 1957. On June 15, 1958 he was promoted as Assistant Engineer. On July 31, 1959 he was appointed as Assistant Executive Engineer. The first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated August 17, 1958 passed by the Corporation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Corporation had no power to fix the age of retirement of its employees. The second respondent challenged the order of the High court in this Court. The appeal was allowed and the judgment of the Division Bench was set aside. The question whether the Corporation could have fixed the age at 60 years for the employees who were employed prior to the date of the impugned order was not raised before the Tribunal. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The decision of the Supreme Court in the case of the Life Insurance Corporation of India vs C. K. Mathew & Ors., [ 1978 ] 1 S. C. R. 10 81, relied upon. 2. The contention that the age should be fixed at 60, is not correct. The age of superannuation has been fixed at 58 years. The Corporation has been constituted under the Act. The Act does not provide for any age limit for the Corporation to fix. The maximum age of the employees is 55 years. There is no provision for fixing the age limit. The employees of a Corporation are governed by statutory rules. The Rules framed under the Corporation Act do not prescribe any age of compulsory retirement. The rule making authority is not bound by the rules. Therefore, the age prescribed by the Rules cannot be altered by the executive instructions.

The appellant was a member of the Bar Association. He had been t aught to be in the profession of a Judge and he had no personal interest in the matter. The respondent, who was an advocate, was not a party to any of the proceedings before the High Court. In the absence of any allegation that the appellant committed contempt of court, it was not open to him to take such a plea. The High Court did not consider the question whether the appellant was guilty of contempt of Court or not. It held that the letter dated April 2, 1975 was not an apology but a mere expression of opinion by the Chief Justice of the High Courts. The letter was addressed to the President of India and not to the Prime Minister. The Chief Justice was not competent to accept the apology. The letters were written by the appellant as well as the Secretary of the State Bar Council. The appellant's case was that the letters were not written by him. The learned Judges of the Division Bench held that there was no contempt of the Court. The appeal filed by the Union of India against the judgment of the Single Judge was dismissed. The appellants have come up in appeal to this Court. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the Supreme Court is not a sentence. [ 243 E ] 2. The contempt jurisdiction is not intended to be used for punishing the contem ner for contempt of courts. The power to punish for contempt is conferred on the Supreme court under Article 129 of the Constitution. [ 244 B ] 3. The powers of the court are wide enough to take care of all possible situations. The court has inherent power to do justice between the parties. The Supreme Court has also the power to make rules for regulating its own procedure. [ 245 C ] 4. The Contempt of Court Act, 1971 is a special enactment dealing with contempt of Courts. Section 15 (1) of the Act provides that every High Court shall have power to regulate its own jurisdiction and power of contempt. [ 246 A ] 5. The provisions of section 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to the High court. The word " Court " in section 14 (1)( b) of that Act means the High. Court. [ 247 D ] 6. The words " any other law " in the context of section 13 (1), which are not relevant for the present purpose, must be read as " the Code ". The word'Court'in section 13 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not defined in the Code. The Code does not contain any provision similar to section 17 of the Indian Penal Code. [ 248 F ] 7. The expression " any person " in sub section (1). of section 12 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, includes a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State and is not remo vable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government. [ 249 G H; 250 A ] 8. The term " Government " in article 12 of our Constitution has been given a very wide meaning. The definition of " State " in clause (c) of article 12 is not exhaustive. The State has the power of making laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India. The Constitution has made a distinction between the two parts of the same section. The first part of article 13 (2) of our constitution is a proviso to article 31 A (1); and second part of that article is a general provision relating to the effect of the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19 (1 (f) and (g) of Part III of the First Schedule to the Constitution of India, and the third part of it is a law relating to preventive detention.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had its registered office at Bombay and it was carrying on business in the State of Maharashtra. The petitioner's company was incorporated in the year 1953. The company was assessed to tax for the assessment years 1952 - 53 and 1954 - 55. In the assessment proceedings for the year 1954 - 56, the Income Tax Officer made an order assessing the income of the company as Rs. 1, 50, 000 / and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 2, 00, 000 /- on the company. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but the appeal was dismissed. The Tribunal held that the provisions of section 5 (4) of the Act were not applicable to the case because the question whether the provisions were attracted or not was not decided by the Appellate Tribunal. On appeal, the Tribunal held against the assessee. The High Court held that section 5 of the impugned Act did not apply to the facts of the case and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the provision was not applicable. The appellant contended before this Court that the decision of the Tribunal is erroneous and that it should be set aside. Held, that the power conferred on the Tribunal under section 5 is wide enough to include within its ambit all cases which are pending before the Tribunal. The jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution is limited to seeing that the Tribunals constituted under the Act have been properly constituted and that they have been invested with the powers of a civil court. The expression " any person " in the context means a person who is entrusted with the duty of maintaining a record of his affairs. The word " person " is defined in the Oxford Dictionary of English Law, Vol. I, p. 12 78, as " a person " who is responsible for the conduct of a business of a firm. The term " person ", therefore, has no doubt a very wide meaning. But it is not necessary that the person must be a person in the sense of a jur istic person. The words " person in respect of whom the proceeding is taken " in section 5 are not intended to mean a person other than the person who has the capacity to do the work of the business of the firm. There is nothing in the language of the section which would justify the conclusion that the legislature intended to exclude persons like the appellant from the operation of the provisions relating to the assessment of income. The section does not say that the income derived from the business carried on by the assessee shall be deemed to be the income from the source of the assessee's business. The income arising from the sale of the assets of the appellant cannot be said to be income from business carried out by the appellant. The fact that the appellant was a resident of the place of business of another person, namely, the respondent, could not make the income taxable under the head " business ". The income from which the appellant received the income was assessable to income tax under section 4 of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer, the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and the Appellate Deputy Commissioner found that the assessee was liable to pay tax under the provisions contained in section 4 (3)( b) of that Act. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the profits earned by the respondent were exempt from tax under that section. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that since the income had escaped assessment, the income could not be taxed under section 6 (1) of section 4. The Revenue filed an application under section 66 (1), and the High court held that it was not open to the Tribunal to go behind the order of the Appellate Collector. The question was whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the matter.

The appellant, a Company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, is a company incorporated in India. It was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling of various kinds of goods. In the course of its business it had been carrying on several business es including that of the appellant. The appellant was a company which was registered under section 26 of the Indian In corpor ated Act, 1956. The objects of the company were to promote the development of the industry and to make profits. The object of the Company was to promote its activities as a trade or business. The Company was formed for the purpose of promoting the sale of products of the members of the Federation. The Association was established for the purposes of promoting its activities. The Memorandum of Association of the Association provided that the Association would be entitled to receive from the members such remuneration as may be fixed by the Board. The members of this Association were also paid commission at the rate of Rs. 1 / 2 per month. The amount received by the Association was not included in the total income of the association. The Society was registered with the Registrar of Fir ms, Delhi. The appellants were appointed as agents of the Society. The respondent No. 1 was appointed as an agent of the appellants. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the appointment of the respondent No 1 as an Agent of the Union. The High Court held that the appointment was made by the appellants as agents and not by the Union of India. The appeal was dismissed. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether the appellants are engaged in the business of buying and selling goods is one of fact. The question is whether the activity of the respondents amounts to " business ". [ 319 E ] (ii) The word'business'has been defined in section 2 (5) of the Act to mean any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adv enture or concern in the nature of trade, profession or v ocation. The expression " business " is wide enough to include any trade or profession carried on by an individual or by a firm or a Hindu undivided family. The words " business ", " profession " and " trade " have been used in the definition of " business." The word " business'is not defined in the Act. The word is not confined to the business or profession of the person who carries on the business. It is a word of wide import. It takes within its fold all kinds of business. [ 319 C; 320 A ] (iii) The expression'business ', in the context of the definition, means the business, profession, trade, manufacture, adv enture, etc., and includes the production, supply and distribution of goods and services. The definition of the word'trade'in section 3 (4) of that Act is inclusive. The meaning of the term'business '. is not restricted to the ordinary dictionary meaning of that word. The dictionary meaning is " any trade " or " any business or trade ". The word, therefore, must be given its ordinary meaning. The use of the expression " trade, business " in the sense of the business is not only incidental to the main business but also to some other business or commercial activity. The business is carried on in the same way as the business itself. The mere fact that the business carried on is a trading activity does not necessarily mean that the activity is not carried on with the profit motive. The true test is whether or not the activity has a systematic activity in the field. If the activity falls within the scope of the particular trade, it would be an organised activity. But if it is not so, then the activity cannot be called a trade. [ 320 F H; 321 B ] (iv) The concept of business is different from the concept of partnership.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. It had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50, and it was assessed to tax in respect of the income from the property. The Income Tax Officer held that the amount received by the assessee as compensation for the acquisition of his estate was not taxable under section 4 (1) (b) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, but was assessable to tax under section 10 (2)( xv). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal to the Tribunal, the question referred to the High Court was whether the sum of Rs. 36, 396 / which was paid as compensation to the assessee's predecessor in interest was taxable as agricultural income. The High Court answered the reference in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The payment of Rs 36, 397 / was not an agricultural income within the meaning of section 2 (1)( a) of Income Tax, Act, 1961. [ 704 E ] (ii) The amount of Rs 37, 396 /- was not a capital receipt. The amount was not liable to be taxed as agricultural Income. [ 705 B ] (iii) The amounts were not agricultural income and could not be regarded as agricultural expenditure. [ 706 C ] (iv) The expression " agricultural income " is not defined in the Act. The word " agricultural " has not been defined in any statute. The definition of agricultural income given in section 2 of the Act is wide enough to include all kinds of agricultural land. The words " agricultural produce " are not defined. The expression'agricultural produce'is defined in section 3 (1), and includes all lands used or occupied for the purpose of agriculture, hor ticulture, animal husband ry, dairy far ming, poultry far ming etc. [ 707 D ] (v) The word'agricultural'is not confined to agricultural land alone. The term'agricultural land'is also not defined anywhere in the Code. The dictionary meaning of the word'agriculture'is " agricultural land ". The word is not restricted to agricultural purposes. The use of the expression'agriculture ', therefore, does not make it clear that the word " agriculture " is wider than the word. The mere use of these words would not make the word agricultural land redundant. [ 708 G H; 709 A ] (vi) The words'agricultural income'have no significance in the context of the definition of the term'agriculture '. The word agricultural'means agricultural land and includes land used for the cultivation of the crop. If the land is used for agricultural purposes, it will be deemed to be agricultural land even though it may be used for non agricultural purposes and not for agricultural purpose. [ 709 F ] (vii) The term " agricultural purpose " is very wide and includes the use of land for the purposes of agriculture. The object of the provision is to provide for the use and occupation of the land for agricultural or any other purpose. The fact that the land has been used for agriculture or for the common purposes of the village or villages is immaterial. [ 710 E ] The word ` agricultural'in section 5 (1). The word has been defined to mean'agricultural or'as such'and the word has not only the meaning assigned to it in the definition clause. The meaning of'agricultural purpose'is derived from the definition in section 6 (1); and the expression is not limited to agricultural or for agricultural use. The explanation to the definition shows that the expression " agriculture or hor ticulture " is used in the sense of the use to which the land was being put at the time of the commencement of the relevant Act.

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors'A'and were promoted to the post of Chargeman Grade II on different dates in pursuance of a circular dated 6th November, 1962 issued by the Director General of Ordnance Factories, Government of India. In accordance with the said circular, the appellants were given promotion as Chargeman Grade I w. e. f. 1. 4. 1967 and they were also granted the same pay scale as that of Chargeman Gr. II. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the aforesaid order of the State Government dated 4th April, 1983. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellants had been given the benefit of the higher pay scale of Rs. 10, 000 /- which was given to them under the Rules and that the respondents were entitled to get the same benefit from the date of their initial appointment as Chargeman Gr.- II. It further held that the action of the respondents in not granting the benefit to the appellants was arbitrary and discriminatory and directed the respondents to grant the same benefits to the petitioners. The State of Madhya Pradesh preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal of the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. 1 The appellants are entitled to be treated as Chargeman's Grade II w. r. t. the date they have been given promotion to the posts of Chargeman II. [ 11 E ] 2. 1 In view of the fact that the appellant has been given a higher pay scales than the respondents, it is not necessary for the appellants to go into the question whether the respondents can be given the same relief as was granted to the other appellants in the case of the present appellants. [ 12 B ] 2 2. 2. The respondents cannot be denied the benefit merely because they have not been given such a benefit. [ 13 D ] 3. 1 There is no dispute that the respondent No. 1 was given the higher scale of pay w. ef. 1 / 1 / 75 - 1 / 8 / 89 and he was given a lower scale of the pay scale. Therefore, the respondents could not be given any benefit of higher pay. [ 14 G ] 3, The appellants have been granted the higher grade pay scale w. p. c.

The appellant, a private operator, was granted a permit by the Karnataka State Transport Authority for plying his tourist vehicle on a route which had been notified as a tourist vehicle. The permit was valid upto 31st March, 1984 and it expired in May, 1985. The appellant filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the appellant was entitled to preference under section 63 (7) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of the Motor Vehicles Act is that every person who has been granted a stage carriage permit should have an opportunity of being heard before he is granted such a permit. [ 10 B ] 2. The object of the proviso to section 63 is to enable the State Transport Undertaking to obtain permits from the Regional Transport Authority or the Regional Authority for the purpose of carrying out its functions under the Act and not to grant any permit to others. It is clear that the proviso does not require that the State Government must give reasons for granting the permit. The power conferred upon the State transport undertaking to grant a stage carriages permit is only to enable it to operate the tourist vehicles. [ 11 C D ] 3. The proviso to sub section (7), which provides that no permit shall be granted unless the applicant has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action, shows that the intention of the legislature was to make the provision mandatory. [ 12 E F ] 4. The words " for the purposes of this Act " in section 68 A (1) are wide enough to include within their scope the application of the provisions of the section. The word'may'used in the proviso is not restricted to the use of the words " in the case of a permit ". The words'in the context of the relevant provisions of section 68 F (1)( a) of Chapter IV A of the Central Act are of wide import and they do not cover the same field. The expression'in respect of the specified routes'in section 2 (8) of that Act means'in relation to the routes covered by the said sections '. [ 13 G H; 14 A ] 5. The definition of'route'in Section 2 (29) of Act is very wide and includes all places where the motor transport service is provided with a view to carry passengers and goods. The term'route ', therefore, cannot be construed to mean a place where the road is situated. [ 15 E ] 6. The contention that the words'route or area'in clause (b) of section 2 of the Kerala Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1963, would apply to the present case, is also devoid of substance. The question whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit of the exemption notification issued under section 64 (1). The appellant is not entitled to claim the benefit under the notification.

The respondent purchased a business from the appellant firm. The sale was effected by the appellant on October 5, 1956 and the respondent paid sales tax on the turnover of the said business. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order. The High Court held that the transaction was not one of sale but of an agreement to sell and therefore the provisions of section 2 (b) of the Act were not attracted. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " sale " in section 2 of the Sale of Goods Act means " any transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration ". It was further contended that the word " sale ", as used in section 3 (1) of that Act, means " transfer of title in goods ". The contention was that the words " transfer " and " sale of goods " are wide enough to include within its ambit the transfer of the right to use goods. HELD: (i) The definition of " sale'in section 4 (1)( a) of Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 is very wide and includes within its scope all kinds of transfers of property made in pursuance of a contract of sale. [ 664 B ] (ii) The word " transfer ", in section 6 (1), does not mean " transfer ". The word'transfer'has been defined in section 5 (1). The word transfer is defined in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which reads as follows: " Transfer of property " means the transfer, by way of mortgage, charge, lease or other transfer of immovable property, or in any other manner whatsoever, including a transfer of such property in favour of a person, whether such person is a registered dealer or not." The word "' transfer " is defined under section 2 sub clause (c) of section 5 of the Tamil Nadu General Clauses Act, 19 04. Section 5 (a) defines " transfer'thus: " transfer, in the case of a transfer, means the transferring of the property in the goods for a price paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under a contract, or otherwise, and includes also a transfer. " The word is defined as meaning " transfer. of property ". The term " transfer is not defined in this Act. The word has been given the wid est possible meaning in the context of the definition of the word in the Act. But the word'purchase'in the definition is not restricted to the transfer. The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive. The words " in the course of trade " do not necessarily mean " in connection with the transfer ". Therefore, the word transfer must be construed in the sense of the transfer itself. The transfer of goods is not a transfer for a money consideration. The question is whether the transfer is a sale of the goods. The expression " in respect of " is not sy non y mous with the expression'transfer '. The word may have different meanings in different context s. The first part of the section says that the transfer shall be deemed to have been made in the ordinary course of business. This is clear from the second part of section 8 (1); but the second proviso to section 8 makes it clear that the sale of any goods shall be treated as a sale in the State if the goods are transferred to the State Government. The third part of this section provides that the State may, by notification, declare that the goods shall not be sold. The goods are specified in the Schedule to the Act and the goods mentioned therein are those which are specified as being subject to a tax under the Act, and the Act is applicable to the goods specified in Schedule I. The Act is a self contained Code.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the G ondal State of Saurashtra. He was suspended from service on February 2, 1955 and he was served with a charge sheet dated March 6, 1954. On March 7, 1954, he was suspended by the Inspector General of Prisons, Gujarat State, under section 60 (1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. The order of suspension was made on February 4, 1955. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of his suspension. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order was not passed by the Government but by the Governor of Gujarat. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition because the order impugned before them was an order of dismissal and that the appellant could not be said to have been removed from service without complying with the provisions of article 311 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The order terminating the services of the appellant was not a punishment within the meaning of article 31 (2) of Constitution. It is true that the word " removal " in article 31 has not been defined in the Constitution but it has been used in the sense of " termination of service ". But there are certain well known rules which govern the interpretation of the expression " removal from service " in articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution. The words " removal or dismissal " do not mean " removal ", nor " removal ". The word " dismissal " means removal from employment. The word'dismissal'in the context means removal or reduction in rank. The expression " dismissal ", therefore, does not mean dismissal or removal from the service. The question whether the dismissal is by way of punishment or otherwise is a matter of discretion. There can be no doubt that the power to dismiss a servant is conferred on the authority competent to dismiss him. The power to punish a servant for misconduct is conferred upon the authority who imposed the penalty of dismissal or remove him from service. If the order is one of dismissal, the order would be one of removal from office. The mere fact that the officer may be removed from the office by the President or the Governor does not make him a member of the service or the Government servant. The Government servant is entitled to the protection of article 310 of the constitution. [ 10 56 A ] (ii) The word ` dismissal'is not sy non y mous with the term'dismissal '. The word dismissal is not a technical or formal expression of the kind of punishment. The phrase ology of the rule is wide enough to include a case where the order has been passed by an authority subordinate to the Government. The rule of natural justice cannot be applied to such a case. The respondent was a temporary government servant and was dismissed from service by the Secretary of State for reasons which were beyond his control. The State of Bombay v. R. M. D. Cham ar b aug wala, [ 1959 ] Supp. 1 S. C. R, followed. (iii) The words'dismissal ', in the first part of the definition of'dismissal, must be read as'dismissal from service'and the second part of that definition is not exhaustive of the word'removal'and that it is only when the order itself is passed by a body of persons other than the Government, that the Government can take action against the person concerned. The decision of the Government is final and conclusive. The respondents were not guilty of any misconduct. The appeal must fail.

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal mines in the year 1932. The respondents were in possession of the said coal. They had been using it for the last several years and they were paying rent to the appellant. In the year 1941, the appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondents on the ground that the respondents had encroached upon the land belonging to them and that the appellant had no right to remove the same. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants had encroached over the land which was lying vacant and that there was no evidence to show that the appellants had encroached on the land. The High Court held that the plaintiff's case was not established by the evidence on record and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The finding of the courts below that the respondent had encroached into the land is based on the evidence and cannot be sustained. [ 529 A ] (2) The burden of proof is on the person who alleges encroachment. It is not necessary that the person claiming adverse possession must prove that he has acquired title to the property. If he does so, he must establish his possession of hostile title to that property. [ 530 B ] (3) The onus is on him to prove that the defendant had taken the law in his own hands. He has to prove his possession or his possession as a trespasser. [ 531 E ] (4) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [ 532 D ] (5) The appellant did not produce any evidence to prove the fact that the disputed area was in his possession. [ 533 C ] (6) The High Courts have rightly held that since the appellant failed to prove this fact, the question of limitation would not arise.

The appellant was a workman of the respondent company. He was dismissed from service by an order dated June 25, 1958. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the termination of his services was not in accordance with the provisions of section 33 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act and therefore the termination was bad. Held, that the order terminating the services of the appellant was illegal as he had no right to continue in service after the termination. It was not open to him to contend that the action taken under section 33 was mala fide or that it was mala fides. The order of dismissal was passed on the ground that the employer had failed to comply with the requirements of section 31 (2). The order was made on the basis of the allegations made against the employee and the evidence adduced before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the enquiry was vitiated because the employer did not produce any evidence to show that the employee had been guilty of misconduct. The management's case was that the appellant had not produced any evidence before the tribunal to prove the charges. The appellant had failed in proving the charge. The finding of the Tribunal that the inquiry was vitiated was based on no evidence. The decision of the High Court is correct.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was granted a lease of the theatre in the town of Ahmedabad for a period of three years. On November 27, 1954, the receiver's of the said theatre were appointed by the Court to take possession of the cinema and to sell it. The receiver's were also authorised to enter into an agreement with the appellant for the sale of the cin emato graph films. The appellant filed a suit against the receiver for a declaration that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 was not binding on him as he had no right or interest in the theatre and that the receiver was entitled to exercise his rights under the agreement. The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether a particular agreement is enforceable in law or not must be decided by the court in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. [ 442 E ] (ii) The agreement dated November 27. 1954, which was executed between the parties, did not contain any provision for the grant of a licence to the appellant. It was only a licence for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the Cinema. The agreement was not merely a licence but a contract. The terms of the agreement clearly indicated that the licence was to be given to the respondent for the performance of certain acts and things which would be done by the appellant in pursuance of the agreements. The respondent could not have been permitted to do so because the agreement was a lease. [ 443 G H; 444 A ] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by the respondent. [ 445 B ] (iv) The appellant was entitled only to the benefit of the covenant contained in the agreement and not to the other reliefs prayed for. [ 446 C ] (v) The order of the High court cannot be sustained.

The respondent was appointed as a Secretary in the District Sol di ers Board of the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed on contract basis for a fixed term of one year and he was paid salary upto 30th of August, 1985. On his appointment, he was given an extension of service till 30th of September, 1985 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. In the meantime, the respondent was reinstated in service on 30th of July, 1985 and he continued to work till 30th August, 1986. The respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination dated 30th of November, 1984. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the order passed by the Governor under Article 309 of the Constitution of India is not an order of confirmation but only an order confirming the order and it could not be said that the respondent had been confirmed in service. It further held that the petitioner was entitled to continue in service till the end of the period of probation and that the impugned order of the Governor was illegal. The appellant has challenged the judgment of the High court in this appeal. Allow ing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of appointment issued in favour of the respondent is not in accordance with law. [ 243 E ] 2. The appointment of the Respondent was made in accordance to the provisions of the Rules. The rules do not provide for any such appointment. The Government cannot appoint a person without following the procedure prescribed under the Rules or without giving him an opportunity of being heard. [ 244 B ] 3. The power conferred upon the Governor by Rule 4 (2) of the U. P. Fundamental Rules is not absolute and is subject to the conditions laid down therein. The Governor can exercise the power of appointing a person on probation and the same is subject, however, to the condition that the person so appointed shall have to undergo the prescribed training and pass the examination within a period of two years from the date of appointment. [ 245 C ] 4. The word'may'used in the rule does not mean'may '. The words'may ','may,'and'may not'mean'must'and not'must '. The word " may " means'may ". [ 245 G ] 5. The expression'may " in the context of the rules is not sy non y mous with the word'shall '. The rule of'may or may not be construed as'may in the sense of'must ', but it is a general rule which is applicable to all cases. [ 246 A ] 6. The words " may ", " or " may not " are used in a statute. The rule is not a rigid rule. The language of the statute is plain and unambiguous. There is no room for any intendment. There can be no doubt that the intention of the legislature is that the rule should be applied in the case of appointments made in pursuance of the rule. [ 247 D ] 7. The proviso to section 3 (1) of U. A. Act provides that the provisions contained in the Act would apply to the appointment of a person who is appointed to the post in the service of the Central Government. The provision in the proviso to sub section (1)( b) of section 3 of the Act makes it clear that the appointment is to be made in the manner provided in the rules. The second proviso to the said section provides that if the appointment in the first instance is made in consultation with the Commission, the Commission shall make its recommendations. The Commission is required to consider the recommendation of the Commission. The recommendation of a Committee constituted under the proviso is binding on the Government. [ 249 F ] 8. The scheme of the proviso shows that the Commission is empowered to make the appointment.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I. P. C. and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was also convicted under Section 302 I, I. PC. and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence of death to one of life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1, 000 /-. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court erred in law in reversing the acquittal of the accused; (ii) the evidence of the eye witnesses should have been believed as they were interested witnesses and their evidence could not be relied upon without corroboration; and (iii) the trial court had wrongly rejected the evidence regarding the presence of the deceased at the time of occurrence and the prosecution case was doubtful. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the medical evidence did not establish the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt. [ 366 E ] (2) The evidence of P. W. 3 who is an injured witness cannot be accepted as he was a chance witness. It is true that his evidence has to be considered with caution because the testimony of the injured witness is not corroborated by other independent evidence. But the fact remains that the injuries found on the person of the victim are possible by the same weapon which was used by the assailants. [ 367 D ] (3) The medical evidence does not support the prosecution version. There is no reason why the evidence given by the injured witnesses should be discarded. [ 368 G ] (4) The prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts. [ 369 B ] (5) The defence version that the deceased was assaulted by the accused persons is not acceptable. The evidence shows that the accused had inflicted two blows on the deceased. The first blow was given by him when he fell down and thereafter the second blow was inflicted by the appellant. The third blow was caused by the deceased after he fell on the ground. The injury report Ex. P / 9 shows that there was fracture of the skull bone. The doctor's evidence shows the following injuries: " 1. Incised wound over the left side of the chest, 2. 5 cm x 1 / 2 cm. X muscle deep. 3. Incised wounds over the right side of chest, 4. 5 cms. x 1. 5. 5 " x 1 " x. 5 ". The Doctor opined that the injury No. 1 was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. [ 370 A ] (6) The injuries Nos. 2 and 3 were simple in nature. The injuries No. 2 & 3 were caused by hard and blunt object. The deceased died due to shock and haemor rhage. The post mortem examination showed that the death was due to the head injury. The Doctor further stated that the cause of death was asphy xia due to strang ulation. The postmortem report shows that all the injuries were ante mortem in nature and the cause was due the death.
