The appellant was a Judge of the High Court and he was appointed as a Judge in the Supreme Court. He was, however, not appointed by the President under Article 124 (4) of the Constitution. On his appointment as a judge of the Supreme court, he was to be paid a salary of Rs. 1, 000 per month. In addition to this, he had been paid a monthly salary of about Rs. 2, 500 per month, which was also included in the salary bill of the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the constitution inasmuch as it was passed without any authority of law and therefore void. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to the protection of article 311 of the Con stitution. It further held that the provisions of section 5 (1)( c) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 were unconstitutional and invalid because they did not provide for any protection against the conviction of an accused person for criminal misconduct. The appeal preferred by the State was allowed and the judgment of the trial court was set aside. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The expression " public servant " used in clause (e) of section 2 of the Prevention of corruption Act, 1988 is wide enough to include a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State and is not remo vable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government. [ 216 A ] (ii) The word'public servant'has been defined in section 2 (c) to mean a public servant who is a member of the Indian Civil Service and is appointed to perform the duties of a public nature. The expression'public servants'is not defined in the Act. But the definition of the term'public officer'in section 3 (c), includes every officer of the Central Government or a State Government. The word " public officer " is defined in clause 2 (d) of s. 2 of Act, which reads as follows: " 2 (e).'public official'means a public officer who is entrusted with the duty of maintaining, superv ising and controlling the public affairs of a state or of any other State; (f)'public service'means any service of a description which is made available to public and not merely to the individual concerned. The definition of'public office'in the context of the present case is not exhaustive but only illustrative. The meaning of the expression'office'is given in the dictionary of the word'office '. The word is not a word of art. It is a word used in the sense of'office ', which means'office of profit '. The expression is used in its ordinary connotation in the Web ster's Dictionary of English Language. The dictionary meaning of'the word is'as'to have,'to hold office '.'to carry on business or profession '. The meaning is derived from the context in which the word has been used in section 5 of the Act, and the context shows that the word must be understood in the light of the context. The question whether a particular office is an office of public nature would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the office is held by a public authority, it is not an office. The test is whether the public servant is holding the office and the members are holding it for the time being. The nature of the office of the public office is a matter of inference to be drawn from the facts of the case. The distinction between a public office and a public corporation is well known. There is no difference between a private and a statutory body. The words'office is not merely a part of the statute creating the office.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. He belonged to a Scheduled Caste. His name was included in the list of voters for the purpose of election to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on various grounds, including that he had not been given a certificate of being a member in the scheduled caste. The High Court held that the appellant was not a member and therefore could not be declared as a member. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " excluding him " in item 40 of Part I of Schedule II of the Constitution means only those persons who are members of the Scheduled Castes specified in the Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950. It was further urged that the word " include " in the context of article 341 (1) of the constitution must be read as meaning " any person or class of persons ". Held: (i) that the words " includes " in article 341 were wide enough to include persons who were not members of a Scheduled Tribe within the meaning of article 342 (1). (ii) that there was no warrant for the view that the term " include ", in article 342, is confined to persons who have been included in a State List. (iii) that in the absence of any definition in the Constitution, the word'include'would mean only such persons who belong to a particular caste. (iv) that if the word includes'in article 340 (1), the word include'in the article would also include persons belonging to a different caste but not all. (v) that even if the words'include ', in article 366 (2) are construed to mean'include '. (vi) that where the word is used in the articles in the same sense, the words are not qualified by the word, and they are used in a restricted sense. (vii) that when the word has been used in article 367 (2), the words have been used to den ote the person who is a member or a non member of a tribe, and the word does not necessarily refer to a person who belongs to a tribe which is not a sub tribe. (viii) that a person cannot be regarded as a person merely because he is a non - member of another caste.

The appellant and the respondent No. 1 were in possession of a flat, which was let out to the appellant by the landlord for his residence. The appellant had been paying rent to the respondent as well as to the landlord. The respondent No 1 filed an application under section 18 (1) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for the eviction of the appellant from the premises on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises as a tenant. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 19 (1)( f) of that Act. He also held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was in any way connected with the business carried on by him. In appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the finding of the Rent Controller that the relationship between the parties was that of landlord and tenant was not correct. It was further urged that the question whether the appellant had sub let the premises or not did not arise because the appellant's case was that the tenancy was terminated by the respondent without notice. Held, that the order of the High court was correct and that the High. Court was right in holding that the termination of the tenancy by the appellant amounted to a breach of the terms of the contract of tenancy. The fact that the landlord had obtained possession of the property by virtue of the agreement of lease does not make the transaction one of lease. The mere fact that a person is in possession would not make him a lessee. The word " lease " in the context means a transfer of the right to enjoy the property. The expression " lease ", in the present case, is not defined in the Transfer of Property Act but is used in the sense of a lease. A lease is a transfer by operation of law. The words " lease of immovable property " are not sy non y mous with " lease ". The definition of the term " lease'in the Indian E ase ments Act, 1882, is very wide and includes a lease of land or building. The definition shows that the lease must be for a period of 30 years. The term " Lease " has been defined in section 2 (d) of this Act as meaning " a lease in respect of a building or part of a house." The definition in the General Clauses Act, 1897, defines " lease in the following terms: " " lease, " is a lease, where the transfer of an interest in the property is made for a certain time, say, a fixed period or the happening of some future event, such as a suit or proceeding in respect thereof. The lease may be either express or implied. The period of the lease is not the same as the period of lease, but the duration of the said lease is fixed by the deed. The intention of the parties is that the lessee should have the right of renewal of the licence. The right of the lessor to terminate the lease at any time during the subsistence of the period is not a right to the lessee. It is a right in the lessor's property. If the lessee is a lessee, the right is extinguished by the act of the lessee, and the lessor is bound to pay the rent to him. The lessee is liable to pay rent to his lessor. The lessor is entitled to recover possession of all the premises occupied by the lessee from the lessee and the lessee has to pay to the lessor the rent of the demised premises for the period. The question is whether the lessee can be evicted from the demised property. There is no doubt that the lessor has the right in favour of the tenant. But the lessee cannot be evicted except in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Act provides for the payment of compensation for the use and occupation of any premises.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the construction of a building on the land belonging to it and in consideration thereof, the respondent agreed to pay Rs. 5 lakhs as compensation for the work done by it. The respondent paid the amount of Rs. 2 lakhs to the appellant company. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent claiming that the respondent was liable to pay the said sum of Rs, 5 lakhs. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under the Act. In appeal, the High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and dismissed the same. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the award of the Tribunal was erroneous because it did not consider the question whether the respondent is entitled to the benefit of the revised wage scales or not. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly rejected the claim of the appellant. [ 177 E ] 2. The High Court was right in its conclusion that the order of the Industrial Tribunal was correct. [ 178 G ] 3. The award of Rs 5 lakhs was made on the basis of the recommendations of the Wage Board which was accepted by the Government. The Labour Court had also taken into account the fact that the workmen were getting more than Rs. 50 / per month. The Industrial Tribunal had given cogent reasons for accepting the contention of the respondent that the increase in the wages was due to the rise in the cost of living index. [ 179 D ] 4. The finding of the High court that the employer was not justified in raising the demand of the workmen is based on the evidence on record. The evidence shows that the employees were getting higher wages at the rate of Rs 100 /- per month and there was no dispute about the same and therefore, the Tribunal should have granted the relief. [ 180 B ] 5. The Award of the Labour Court is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, was awarded certain contracts for the supply of food grains to its employees. The contract provided that the wages prescribed by the award would be paid at the rate fixed by the Government and in accordance with the terms of the contract. The respondent workmen raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the rates of wages fixed by it were not justified as they were not fixed by reference to the wage structure prescribed by it. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that though the rates fixed by an award could be revised by the appropriate Government, the same had been made applicable to all the employees of the company. In this appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The question whether the wages fixed under the award can be revised or not is a matter of discretion of the Labour Court. [ 422 C ] (2) The power conferred on the Labour Courts under section 15 of the Act is wide enough to include within its ambit the powers conferred on them by sections 23 and 29 of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is true that the words " any other law for the time being in force " in section 2 (vi) are wide enough and must be construed liberally so as to include therein the provisions of the said Act. But the scope of the power conferred upon the Labour courts under section 2 is limited to the extent of the application of the provisions contained in the said section. [ 423 D E ] (3) Section 2 (v) does not confer any power on the labour court to make any alteration in the conditions of service of the workmen employed by the employer. The power to make such alterations is given only to the authority specified in the Act. [ 424 F G ] (4) The object of the legislature in enacting the Act was to provide for the regulation of the conditions and the manner in which the conditions laid down in the award should be regulated. The object was to prevent exploitation of the workers and to ensure that the conditions imposed by the awards were fully complied with. [ 425 B ] (5) The expression'conditions of employment'has been used in the sense of'conditions'and therefore the word'conditions ', in the context, means'conditions '. The expression " conditions of work " is defined in section 3 (b) of the, and includes the conditions in respect of which the employer may make an order of discharge or dismissal. The definition of'wages'in section 4 (1)( b) is wide and comprehensive. The term'wages " is not confined to the basic pay drawn by the employee but also includes dearness allowance. [ 426 H; 427 A ] (6) The word'wages ', in its ordinary connotation, is not restricted to the minimum wages payable to the employee. It includes the value of the goods supplied by the employers to the employees. If the expression'wages is not defined in the statute, it is difficult to see how the meaning of the word " wages " can be ascertained without any difficulty.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, and he was charged with criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51, 000. He was tried by the Special Judge, who acquitted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish the charge against him under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the sanction was necessary as it was not obtained before the appellant could be prosecuted under section 409 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The sanction is required under section 197 (1), Cr. P. C., for prosecution of the appellant for offences under sections 465, 467, 471 and 477 A of the I. P., Code of Civil Procedure. [ 10 31 B ] (2) The offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery is one which is covered by section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It is not every offence committed by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, but of a person who holds an office under a State Government or of a local authority, established by or under any law made by Parliament. The question whether the act complained of is done in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of the State has to be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 11 E F ] (3) The expression " official duty " in section 197 does not mean a duty to do something, but includes the duty to act according to the rules of conduct applicable to the public servants. The word'official duty'in section 196 (1)( c) means a duty imposed by the statute upon a public officer. The expression'official duties'in the context of section 197, therefore, must be construed in the light of the context in which they are used. [ 12 G H; 13 A ] (4) Section 197 (2)( b) of the Cr. PC. is not confined to cases where there is no official duty to perform. The words'official acts'in sub section (1). are not qualified by the words'act'or'duty'as defined in section 5 of the Act. The section does not say that the act should be done in any particular manner. The act must have been done in pursuance of the duty. The accused may be charged with the aid of section 196 of the Penal Code, but if he is found guilty of the offence of cheating, he can be convicted of the said offence. [ 13 D, 14 B, C, D, E, F, G, H, 15 A, C. A.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore and Cochin. It had its registered office in the former Cochin State, which was later merged with the United States of Travancore. In 1949 the assessee company was assessed to income tax under section 3 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not liable to be taxed as an individual for the assessment year 1948 - 49 but he was entitled to deduct from his profits and gains the amount of Rs. 79, 275 which was the amount received by him as a result of the sale of the shares of the company. The High Court on reference held that it was not necessary to consider whether the assessee had any other source of income or not. The question referred to the High Court was answered in favour of the Revenue. The assessee appealed to this Court. Held (per Sinha, C. J., Shah, J.): (i) The words " business in British India " in section 2 (15) of the Act are wide enough to include within its ambit the activities carried on by the assessee in the course of his business. The word'business'is not defined in the Act. The expression'business in the Indian Act means the business in which the assessee carries on the business. But the definition does not say that the business must be carried on in the sense in which it has been used in the definition. The meaning of the word'activity'is derived from the dictionary meaning of'business '. The word is not confined to the actual carrying on of the business but includes the entire activity of the assessee. The words'business ','carried on'and'carried out'have been used inter change ably in the context of the definition of the term'business. [ 271 B ] (ii) The word " business " in the first part of the section means the carrying on, in the ordinary sense, of the same kind of business, that is, the business of the person who carries on that business. If the business is carried on, then the business would be deemed to be carried out in the usual way of business. There is no reason why the word " carried on " should not be given the meaning of that word. The second part of section 2 of the, Act, therefore, refers to the business carried on and not to the carrying out of the main business. It is clear that the word business in section 10 of the Income Tax Acts of 19 18 and 19 18, and the word in the second part thereof, were used in connection with the business and not in the same sense as the word used in section 4 of the English Act. [ 272 A, D, E, F, G, H, 273 A, C, D ] (iii) The expression " business ", in section 5 of the Travancore General Clauses Act, 11 of 18 86, means the whole business of a dealer in the United King dom. The first part, of section 5, of which the word is used in sections 2 (1)( a), 2 (b) and 2 (c) of that Act, defines the word, " business ". The word, in section 3 (1) of this Act, is not only the word of the first clause, but also the word. In the present case, the word has been defined in section 6 of the General Clauses (1), (2) and (3) of section 3. The third part of that section is not relevant for the purpose of the present appeals. The fourth part of s. 5 of that Part of the said Act, which deals with the subject matter of the other provisions of the Constitution, is in the nature of a proviso to article 286 (1).

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1946. It had a branch office at Calcutta and its branches were situated at Calcutta. In the year 1947, the respondent company entered into an agreement with the appellant company for the retirement of its employees. The company agreed to pay the age of superannuation at 60. The Company's case was that it had been doing business in India since 1948 and that there was no question of any future increase in the age. The Tribunal held that the age was fixed at 60 and not at 60 as contended by the appellant. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal has rightly found that the appellant had been able to establish that the retirement age of the workmen was fixed on the basis of the prevailing practice in the Bombay region. [ 430 E ] (2) The fact that the Tribunal had accepted the evidence of the parties before it is not sufficient to justify the conclusion that the tribunal had committed any error in fixing the age at 60 or at 60, because the Tribunal has taken into account all relevant factors including the age factor. [ 431 B ] (3) The High Court was right in holding that the award of the Tribunal was correct. [ 432 D ] (4) The finding of the High Court that the decision of the Industrial Tribunal that the date of retirement should be fixed at 58 is erroneous. The High court was wrong in taking this view. [ 433 A ] (5) The contention that the High court erred in making the award without giving any reasons cannot be accepted. The award of a Tribunal is binding on the parties and the Tribunal is bound to give effect to it. [ 434 G ] (6) The award made by the Tribunal does not suffer from any infirmity. [ 435 C ] (7) The Award of the Appellate Tribunal is based on the evidence adduced before it and the findings recorded by the Industrial Court are not perverse. The finding recorded by it is a finding of fact which could not be disturbed in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [ 436 F ] (8) The order of the Labour Court is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the High. Court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. [ 437 H;

The company was registered in the year 1961 and had been carrying on business of manufacturing, selling and dealing in various products. It was also a subsidiary of M / s. L. A. Mit che ll Ltd., which was incorporated in the name of M. K. Gupta & Co. as its Managing Director. In the year 1965 the appellant company was incorporated with the object of acquiring and holding shares in the company. The appellant company acquired the shares of the company by virtue of the powers conferred upon it under section 237 (b) of the Companies Act, 1956. The Company Law Board held that the appellant was guilty of fraud, mis feas ance and other misconduct and directed the company to pay compensation to the shareholders for the loss caused to them. The company filed an appeal before the High Court against the order of the Company Law Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. 1 The appellant is not entitled to any relief because the company has not been able to establish that there were any acts of oppression or mismanagement in the affairs of the appellant. [ 10 31 C ] 2. 2 The appellant's case is that the company was not in existence at the time when the agreement was entered into between the parties. The fact that the agreement did not contain any clause regarding the termination of the agreement would not make the agreement void ab initio. [ 11 32 E ] 3. The question whether the agreement is void or void able does not arise in the present case since the agreement itself was not terminated by the appellant but only by the respondent No. 1. The agreement was executed in the course of the proceedings before the Company law Board. The terms of the contract are binding on both the parties and the appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of the Contract Act. [ 12 31 B ] 4. The contract was entered in the form of a memorandum of understanding and the parties agreed to abide by the terms of it. The Memorandum of Understanding was signed by the parties on May 19, 1965. The letter of the parties dated April 5, 1965 clearly shows that the parties had agreed to refer all disputes arising out of the agreements to arbitration. The parties had expressly agreed that the matter should be referred to arbitration and the arbitrator shall have the power to decide the dispute himself.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. They were also convicted under sections 395 and 397 of the I. P. C. and sentenced each of them to suffer rigorous imprisonment of one year. The High Court, in appeal, confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to three years'rigorous imprisonment. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act could not be drawn against the appellants because they had been acquitted by the trial court as there was no evidence to show that the stolen property was stolen or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated. It was further submitted that the High Court erred in holding that the appellants were guilty of having committed an offence punishable under section 411 of the Penal Code. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The presumption is strong er when the presumption is drawn from the circumstances of the case. [ 722 B ] (2) The fact that the appellant was found with some other person at the time of the dacoity cannot be a ground for drawing the presumption. The fact of recovery of the stolen goods from the possession of the appellant does not necessarily mean that he was aware of the fact that he had purchased the same. If the appellant knew that the said goods were stolen, he would have immediately taken them away. He may have known that the goods might have been stolen. But if the appellant did not know that the ornaments were stolen he would not have kept those goods in his house. [ 723 D E ] (3) The burden of proof is always on the prosecution to prove that the gold which was seized was the stolen article. There is nothing in the evidence to indicate that the articles recovered were the stolen articles. The presumption can be drawn only after the prosecution has established that the items were stolen. [ 724 G H ] (4) The question whether the ornaments belonged to the appellant or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The nature of the ornaments and the manner in which they were kept are matters of evidence. The courts below have rightly held that the prosecution failed to establish that the jewellery was stolen. The ornaments were not stolen. There was no reason why the ornaments should have been kept in the custody of the relatives till such time as the original offenders could take them away from the custody. [ 725 F ] (5) The High Courts have rightly pointed out that the burden of proving that the properties were stolen was on the appellant. [ 726 A ] (6) The onus of proof was on him. The burden was on his shoul ders to show the existence of the circumstances from which the inference could be drawn.

The petitioner was a manufacturer of'th inner'and'th outer'in the State of Delhi. He purchased the said product from the manufacturers of'Th inner'on payment of Rs. 1, 000 /- per month as fee for the purchase of the same. The petitioner paid the fee of Rs, 500 /- to the Government. The Government issued a notification under Section 5 (2) of the Act fixing the fee payable by the manufacturers. The petitioners filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification did not suffer from any infirmity. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned notification is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it does not provide for any reasonable classification between the two classes of persons who are similarly situated. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the legislation is to prevent discrimination against the people who are otherwise equally placed. It is also clear that the object of prescribing the fee is to ensure that the persons who have been subjected to the levy of fees are not left without any remedy. [ 223 E ] 2. The power conferred upon the Government by section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 is an enabling provision and the power has to be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the statute. The Legislature has made the law in exercise of its powers under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The State legislature has no power to make any law which takes away or ab rid ges the right conferred by the Constitution or any other law. The Act is a piece of social legislation and is a measure of social welfare. The provisions of Part III of the constitution are not intended to be exhaustive of the subject matter of the enactment but they are intended to regulate the manner in which the administration of justice is carried on. The question whether the impugned Act is discriminatory or not must necessarily depend upon the nature of the right which is sought to be enforced. [ 224 G H; 225 A ] 3. The impugned notification dated 7. 8. 1973 is ultra vires the Constitution and is liable to be struck down. [ 226 B ] 4. The notification dated 21. 10. 1971 is valid and the same cannot be struck out.

The assessee firm was a firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. It had its head office at Bombay and it had its branch offices at Bombay. The business of the assessee was carried on by the firm in the course of its business. In the year of account, the assessee had a large number of branches in Bombay and the profits were made from those branches. The assessee claimed that the amounts received by it as loans were not capital receipts but were paid to the Bombay firm for the purpose of carrying on the business of money lending. The Tribunal held that the amount was not a capital receipt but an income receipt. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the moneys were paid out of the funds of the partnership and that the assessee's claim that the monies were not borrowed was correct. The High Court also found that the Tribunal had not considered the question whether the amounts were borrowed or not. The question referred was answered in the affirmative and against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (1) the sum of Rs. 2, 68, 385 / was not borrowed by the assessee from the Bombay company; (2) the amounts which were advanced by the Bombay Company to the Madras firm were not the amounts borrowed by it from the Madras company; and (3) the amount of Rs 2, 67, 385 was not the amount borrowed by way of interest on the amounts due to the assessee as a result of the sale of the shares of the company. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The sum of the sum is not a loan or advance given by the Madras Company to any other person. [ 423 E ] (ii) The amount of the loan is not borrowed from the assessee but is borrowed by him from the Calcutta Bank. The amount is not the loan taken by the company from the Allahabad Bank. There is nothing to show in the statement of the case that the money was borrowed by means of the Bombay Bank. [ 424 G ] (iii) The amounts are not borrowed as loans from the bank. The amounts were advanced to the Calcutta Company and the amounts are borrowed by them from the Delhi Bank. Therefore, the amounts cannot be said to have been borrowed by virtue of the transactions between the parties. [ 425 C ] (iv) The fact that the sums were borrowed by one of the partners of the firm from the Punjab National Bank does not make any difference. [ 426 A ] (v) The Tribunal has rightly pointed out that the sum was not advanced by way the amount advanced by a firm to the firm and the same was not utilised by the other partner. [ 427 D ] (vi) The question whether a particular amount was borrowed from a firm or a firm is a question of fact and the Tribunal has to decide the question of law. [ 428 B ] (vii) The finding of the Tribunal that the payments were not made by the appellant to the Punjab firm is not based on the facts and circumstances of the present case. [ 429 F ] (viii) The High Courts have held that in view of the provisions of section 10 (2)( vi) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the payment of the amount by the Punjab company to the appellant was not an expenditure incurred by the appellants. [ 430 H ] (ix) The words " any other business " occurring in section 10 of the Act do not refer to the business carried on the basis of the share capital of the appellant. The word " business " is not defined in the Act. The expression " business ", in section 2 (4) of section 2 of the Companies Act, 1956, means the business in which the company is engaged in the business.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. They filed applications before the Land Acqu is tion Officer for determination of compensation payable to them. The Land Acquisition Officer passed an award on September 20, 1984 determining the market value of the land at Rs. 1, 50, 000 /- per acre. The petitioners challenged the said award in a writ petition before the High Court and obtained interim stay of dispossession therein. The High Court allowed the petitions and directed status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed as the awards were not made within two years from the date of the publication of the declaration under Section 4 of the Act. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The acquisition proceedings have lapsed because the award has been made within the period prescribed by law. [ 10 B ] 2. The notification making the declaration is not a pre condition for the exercise of the power under section 11 A of the. [ 11 C ] 3. The expression " shall be published " in the first proviso to section 11 (1) of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976, means the publication in the Official Gazette of the notification under section 4 of that Act. It is not necessary that the publication should be made before the commencement of the acquisition proceeding. [ 12 D ] 4. The word " shall " used in the second proviso to Section 11 A does not mean that the notification must be published before the expiry of the period of two years mentioned in the third proviso to sub section (1). [ 12 E ] 5. The words " shall not be published ", occurring in the fourth proviso to subsection (1), are mandatory. The requirement of publication of a declaration under section 6 of the 1894 Act is only directory and not mandatory. [ 13 G ] 6. The purpose of the legislature in enacting the Land acquisition Act is to provide for the acquisition of the property of the State Government or its agencies. The object of the enactment is to make provision for the payment of compensation to the owner of the acquired land. The legislature has provided for the compulsory acquisition of such property for public purposes. The Legislature has not laid down any guidelines for the purpose of acquisition of land. [ 14 F ] 7. The scheme of the provisions contained in sections 17 and 19 of the Karnataka Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, makes it clear that the provisions thereof are mandatory and do not apply to acquisitions made after the commencement. [ 15 H; 16 A ] 8. The provisions of section 11 of the Central Act are mandatory in character. The award must be made within a period of one year from the commencement thereof. [ 16 B ] 9. The language of section 11A of the LA Act is very clear and unambiguous. There is no reference in the Special Leave Petitions to any of the notifications issued under section 17 of the L. A. Act. [ 17 D ] 10. The fact that the award was made within three years from September 20 1984 would not make any difference. The Collector's order dated August 14, 1984 is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [ 18 D ] 11. The contention that the awards could not be made beyond the period specified in the notification cannot be accepted. The awards were made within four years from October 20, 1983. The Award was made on September 21, 1984. The appellants did not challenge the validity of the award till September 20. 1984 when the award came into force. The claimants did not file any objections to the award. Therefore, the Special leave Petitions are liable to be dismissed. [ 19 E ] 12. The Special Leave Petition No.

The appellant bank was a bank which had been paying the salary of its employees. It was not in dispute that the Bank had fixed the pay of the two workmen at Rs. 190 and Rs. 1, 000 respectively. The Bank had also fixed the scale of pay of Rs. 175 to be given to the two employees. The appellant Bank had made an application under section 33 C (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act for fixation of the pay on the basis of the scales of pay provided by the Sas try Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The question was whether the appellant bank could fix the pay at Rs, 190 or Rs. 200 per month. The High Court held that the appellant Bank was entitled to fix the scale at Rs., 175 and Rs, 175 as revised from time to time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award of the Labour Court was erroneous because it did not consider the relevant provisions of the Sas ty Award as amended by the Bank. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: (i) The award of Rs, 174 is correct. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) The appellant has been paid Rs. 2, 500 per month as dearness allowance. The amount of Rs., 2, 000 per month is payable to the appellant. The respondent's claim for payment of Rs,. 2, 100 per month cannot be sustained. [ 11 32 D ] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the direction issued by the High Court was justified. [ 12 31 E ] (iv) The order of the High court directing the payment of the amount of the salary to the respondent was set aside. The order was confirmed by the Supreme Court.

The appellant, a trade union of the hotel, was a member of the Association. He had been given certain facilities for the purpose of running a hotel and also for the sale of the land to the hotel. The hotel was constructed by the appellant as a part of its business. It was not a commercial venture but a private one. The appellant was a public limited company. The Chief Minister's speech in the conference of the Hotel was that it would be a commercial concern and the hotel would be run on a commercial basis. The Government decided to lease out the land for the hotel to the appellant. The lease was for a period of three years. The lessee was entitled to sell the land at a price which was fixed at Rs. 1, 000 per month. The State Government was directed to pay the amount of Rs. 2 lakhs to the lessee. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the State Government. The High Court held that the lease was a commercial transaction and the appellant was not entitled to any relief. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the High court was erroneous and should be set aside. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High court has rightly held that there is no evidence to show that the appellant had made any attempt to get the land leased out. [ 280 B ] (ii) The fact that the land was being used for a commercial purpose does not mean that the building was being put up for a profit. If the building is let out for a residential purpose, the same will have to be taken into account. There is nothing to show from the record that the construction was intended to be carried out for the benefit of the owner or the tenant. [ 281 E ] (iii) The appellant had not been able to establish that the structure was being built for the use of the public. The fact remains that the entire area was being utilised for the purposes of the business. The only ground on which the High Courts have relied upon is that the premises were being used as a commercial complex. The question whether the building could be said to be used for the business of the company is a matter of evidence. The mere fact that some of the buildings are used for commercial purposes cannot be a ground for holding that the buildings were not used for any commercial purpose. [ 282 C ] (iv) The building is a commercial activity. The building was constructed for the personal use of a large number of people. The landlord is not expected to go to the common place. The whole building is used for his own residence. The other members of the family are not expected, therefore, to stay in the same house. The appellants have not been denied the right to carry on their business. They have not even pleaded that they are doing so for the last about two decades. [ 283 A ] (v) The first respondent has not been shown to be a person who is not a member or a partner of the firm. The second respondent is a stranger. The third respondent is not an individual. The first appellant is a partnership firm. It is a joint family. The property is owned by the partners. The respondents are not the owners of the property. The properties are not being used by the parties. The fourth respondent is the son of the deceased. The fifth respondent is an un connected with the appellant and the other respondents are the sons of the third respondent. The case of the respondents is that they have been using the premises for the residential purpose. The premises are not used by them for the commercial purpose, but for the other purposes. The business is carried on by the respondents. The main object of the Act is to provide for the protection of the interests of the tenants.

The assessee was a partner in a firm carrying on business of banking and other financial services. He had a fixed deposit with the Bank for Rs. 50, 000. On 1st January, 1957, he made an application to the Income Tax Officer for the transfer of his share in the bank account in the name of his son. The Income Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the amount was not received by him as a loan but it was paid as a gift. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs. 1, 50, 00, 000 was properly included in the income of the assessee and the balance of Rs, 50. 000 was liable to be taxed under section 10 (2) of the Act. In appeal before the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that since the amount of Rs 1, 00. 000 had been transferred to the account of the wife of the deceased, the same could not be treated as a capital receipt. The High Court also held that there was no valid gift by the assessee to his son and hence the amount could not have been included in his income. The Revenue appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amounts were received by the wife and the daughter of the husband of the respondent who was a minor at the time of the marriage and therefore, they were not assessable to tax. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the amount received by way of gift from the wife or the daughter is taxable under section 4 of the Income tax Act, 1961 does not arise in the present case because the amount which was received by her as a donation from the husband was not a capital expenditure incurred by the husband. [ 125 E ] 2. The fact that the assessee had a credit balance of the amount in the books of account of his wife cannot be taken as a circumstance against the assessee. [ 126 C ] 3. The amount received as gift from his wife was not part of the income derived from the property of the father. The assessee's contention that the said amount should be regarded as a part of his income must fail. [ 127 B ] 4. The expression " any other income " used in section 10 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 has to be construed in the light of the definition of the word " income " given in section 2 (6) of that Act. The words " any income " occurring in section 5 (1)( i) of this Act are wide enough to include the amount payable to the assessee in respect of the gifts made by the deceased. [ 128 D ] 5. The word " any " in section 9 (1) of Act, 18 of 1922, means " any payment made by a person to his wife or his wife by way or as a condition of such marriage ". The word'any'in section 8 (1), however, is not defined in the Act and the context in which it occurs in section 7 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, would show that the word'income'in the context of section 10 is to be understood in the sense of the term " income ". [ 129 G H;

The High Court of Orissa, in the exercise of its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, has power to issue directions for the implementation of its orders. In view of the decision of this Court in State of West Bengal vs N rip endra Nath Bag chi (1) and State of Bihar vs N. K. Prasad Singh (2), it is not necessary to go into the question whether the High Court was right in directing that the order of the Government should be implemented by the Government. It is true that the High court had no jurisdiction to direct the Government to implement the order but it could have directed the Government as well as the Registrar of the High Courts to comply with the direction given by the High. Court. But the High, Court did not do so. The High court was not competent to pass any such direction. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant, a co sharer and the co sharers in respect of agricultural land and village immovable property, filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to pre emption under section 15 (1)( b) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to claim pre emption as he had failed to prove his right of pre emption. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 15 of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 and that the decree passed by the trial court was valid. It further held that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer, it was not necessary to give the appellant an opportunity to pay the amount of pre empt or's share of the land. On appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word'other'in section 15 is used in the sense of'other co owners '. [ 123 E ] 2. The expression'other ', in section 16 (1) means'other than the co sharer'and does not include a co owner. [ 124 D ] 3. The words'other " in section 14 are wide enough to cover all the co owners. [ 125 G ] 4. The use of the word'others'in clause fourth ly of section 14 is indicative of the fact that the legislature intended to exclude the co owner from the scope of the term'other '. [ 126 F ] 5. The meaning of the expression'others ', in the context of section 16 is that the expression includes only those who have been given the right to pre empt. [ 127 C ] 6. The definition of'others " in the Act is very clear and unambiguous. The intention of the Legislature is to exclude any person from the purview of the definition of the'other persons'in the case of the present case. [ 128 A ] 7. Section 15 (2) of Punjab Act, 11 of 1953, provides that where a co - sharer has no co sharer in the property, the co - owner shall be deemed to be a co tenant. [ 129 B ] 8. The effect of the amendment of section 18 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, is that if a co sharers are not co sharers, the same would be treated as a class by themselves. [ 130 E ] 9. The object of the provision is to protect the interest of the co tenants. [ 131 H; 132 A ] 10. The provisions of section 13 (1), which provide for the transfer of the interest in the land in favour of the transferee, are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act. [ 133 E ] 11. The right of the appellant to the land is not affected by the provisions contained in section 13 of the said Act. There is nothing in the provisions which prohibits the transfer by the co tenant of the property in favour. of the purchaser. [ 134 E ] 12. The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions in the proviso to section 13.

The alien ees have been in possession of the property from the date of the sale deeds. They are entitled to recover the amount paid by them as mesne profits and also for damages for use and occupation of the properties. The alien ee has not been able to prove that there was any agreement or settlement between the parties, which would bind the alien ees. In view of the fact that the alien ee had no interest in the property, the alien ations were valid and the trans fere es had become owners of the same. The alienation is void and cannot be enforced against the alien ors. The suit filed by the alien ants was decreed on contest. The High Court held that the alienation was valid and binding on the alien ers and the alien es had no right to claim any share in the properties of the alien or. It further held that even if the alien e had no title to the property it could not be said that the transfer was invalid. On appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the matter remanded to the Trial Court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. [ 541 G ] 2. The decree of the trial court is set side and the parties are directed to bear their own costs.

The appellant company was a sick industrial company. It had been declared sick by the Government of India under section 3 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The workmen were not entitled to any leave with retrospective effect from January 1, 1975 and they were not eligible for the benefit of the sick leave. The Company filed an application before the Tribunal claiming that it was entitled to the benefits of the said sick leave as it had not been granted in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Tribunal rejected the claim on the ground that the sick certificate did not contain the necessary particulars regarding the sickness of the workmen and that the workmen were entitled to be paid only the amount of sick leave which was due to them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that the benefit should be given to the workmen in view of the fact that the sickness benefit would be available to the workman in case he is able to establish that the conditions of the sickness are satisfied. [ 10 31 B ] (ii) The question whether the sick industrial unit is entitled to get the benefit or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the condition of the medical treatment is not fulfilled then the benefit will have to be given. [ 11 E F ] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal's order was correct. [ 12 G ] (iv) The contention that the appellants had not produced the medical certificates showing that the employees were not in a position to do so cannot be accepted. The High Courts decision is based on the evidence on record and there is no reason to interfere with the same. [ 13 A ] (v) The finding of the Tribunal that the medical certificate issued by the Medical Officer shows that the appellant had not taken into account the requirements of the scheme of the Factories Act, 1948, is erroneous. The certificate does not show that the concerned workmen were in a fit state of health to work in the factory. The appellant's case is that the respondent No. 2 was not in the employment of the appellant company at all. [ 14 C ] (vi) The appellant has not produced any material to show that it had made any attempt to obtain the requisite certificate. The mere production of the certificate does n't prove that the certificate was genuine.

The appellant was detained under section 3 (1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Sm ug g ling Activities Act, 1974. He was arrested on August 9, 1955. On September 8, 1955, he was taken into custody and produced before the Advisory Board. His detention was confirmed by the Government on October 30, 1955 and the order of detention was served on him on November 4, 1955 in pursuance of the order passed by the State Government under section 10 of the Act. The grounds of detention were communicated to the detenu on December 5, 1955 but no representation was made against it till January 11, 1956. The appellant's representation was rejected by the Central Government on February 12, 1956, and the same was communicated to him on March 13, 1956 and the grounds of rejection were also communicated to his brother. The High Court held that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the question whether or not the petitioner was a person who was likely to be affected by the order and that there was no material to show that the petitioner had been prejudiced because of the non supply of the particulars. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The right to make an effective representation is a valuable right which is guaranteed by article 22 (5) of Constitution. It is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution and is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the legislature in the interest of general public. [ 384 B ] (ii) The power conferred on the detaining authorities under section 2 (b) of C OF E PO SA is a very wide power and must be exercised with great care and caution. The power has to be exercised reasonably and in a rational manner. The object of making the order is to prevent the detenu from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The purpose of the law is to secure the social order and to prevent disturbance of public tranqu ility. The concept of " public order " is a dy namic concept and it cannot be confined to a narrow compass. [ 385 A ] (iii) The expression " public safety " in Article 22 (6) of our Constitution means the security of the State or the maintenance or the public order in the sense that it includes the maintenance, the maintenance and the satisfaction of the detaining Authority as well as the maintenance in the public interest. [ 386 G ] (iv) The words " maintenance of law and order " in clause (b), " maintenance " in the context of the maintenance order, are of wide amplitude and they have to be construed in the light of the context and the background in which they occur. [ 387 D ] (v) The word " maintenance ", in the first part of the definition of " maintenance, " in section 2 of the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971, does not mean " maintenance ". The word'maintenance'in the second part of section 2, therefore, refers to the whole of the " maintenance and control of the public and the maintenance " of the general public " and the latter part of it, and not the maintenance for the maintenance.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army. He was tried by a court mar tial for offences under section 19 of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, which provided for the removal of a person from service, did not apply to him as he was not a member of the armed forces. Held: (1) that r, 14 of Army Rules is ultra vires the power conferred by section 19 read with r. 15 of the Rules. (2) that the words " subject to the provisions of the rules " occurring in r. 13 of the Indian Rules are wide enough to include all persons subject to these rules. (3) that s. 19 of Act No. XX V of 1954, provides that no person shall be removed from the service except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. (4) that sub rule (2)( b) of r. 16 of the said Rules does not provide for any such enquiry but only provides for the procedure to be followed before the order of removal can be passed. (5) that there is no provision in the rules for giving a reasonable hearing to the officer concerned before passing the order. (6) that if the officer is not satisfied with the report of the inquiry officer or the disciplinary authority, he may dismiss the officer from service. (7) that in the present case the officer was not given an opportunity to make his representation against the proposed punishment. (8) that even if the rules were silent about the procedure for imposing the penalty, the rules do not provide that the procedure should be followed. (9) that since the rules did not provide any time limit for the conclusion of the proceedings, the action taken by the authorities could not be challenged. (10) that Rule 14 of Rules, 1955, is ultra virus the powers conferred by the Act. (11) that rule 14 of R. 14 is ultra - vires the powers of the Central Government under section 191 of the.

The appellant company was assessed to octroi duty on the goods brought by it from its factory at the rate of Rs. 1, 000 per ton. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the levy is not justified as there was no provision in the Act or the rules made thereunder which required the imposition of octroi; (ii) the assessment order was bad because the tax had been levied without authority of law and therefore the levy could not be sustained; and (iii) the demand for payment of octroi was illegal. The word " person " is defined in's 2 (e) of that Act to mean a person who is liable to pay the tax. It does not mean that the person must be a person other than the owner of the goods. The appellants were convicted under section 31 (1) read with section 33 of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of six months. They filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conciliation proceedings could not be said to have concluded within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding, as the conciliation officer had no power to make the report after the expiry of 14 days from the date of the order of dismissal. Held: (i) that the Conciliation Officer was bound to make his report within 14 day of the occurrence of the strike; (ii) that in view of the provisions of section 12 (6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the conciliation was deemed to have commenced on the date when the report was received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings did not end when the reports were received by it. The Conciliation Officer had no jurisdiction to make any report under section 12 of the. [ 738 E ] (iii) Section 12 (5) of The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, provides that where a settlement is arrived at between the employer and the workmen otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceedings, the Conciliation officer shall submit his report to the appropriate government. The proviso to section 12 makes it clear that if the conciliation is not completed within 14 working days or within such shor ter period as may be specified by the State Government, the Labour Commissioner may extend the time limit for submission of the report. But the proviso does not say that the report should be submitted within 14 months. It only says that the failure to submit the report within the prescribed period would result in the termination of the proceedings. The words " pendency of conciliation proceeding " are wide enough to include the delay in the completion of the proceeding. The expression " pendency " in section 12 means the cessation of the dispute or the abandonment of the claim by the workman. The word " pendency ", therefore, cannot be construed to mean that the proceedings must be closed even though the report has been made by the Conciliation authority. The decision of the Supreme Court in Workmen of M / s. National Textile Corporation Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [ 1960 ] 2 S. C. R. 806, referred to.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Act on the ground that he had been in detention for more than two years. He was arrested and detained in connection with a criminal case. The grounds of detention were served upon him on the same day, i. e., on 2. 1. 1985. The order of detention was passed on the basis of the report of the District Magistrate, Dhanbad, which was received by the State Government on 3. 1 1. 85. The petitioner's representation against his detention was rejected by the detaining authority on the following grounds: (1) That the detenu was not in custody at the time when the order of preventive detention was made; (2) that there was no cogent material before the detaining Authority to come to the conclusion that the detenu is likely to be released from detention; (3) that the order was not passed as required under section 3 (2)( b) of the said Act; (4) that it was necessary to detain the detenu in order to prevent him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order; (5) that in view of the fact that the petitioner was in jail custody, the order could not have been passed without taking into consideration the relevant factors mentioned in section 3 of the aforesaid Act; and (6) that since the order has been passed after the expiry of three months from the date of the order, the petitioner could not be detained under section 2 (b) read with section 3. In the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the respondents it was stated that the detention order was passed after about one year of the alleged incident and the petitioner had been released on bail in the present case. It was further stated that even if the order dated 18. 2. 1985 was not challenged, the detenu would still be entitled to be set at liberty. The High Court held that the period of detention of the petitioner in this case was only six months and the order passed by the District magistrate was valid and legal. The writ petition filed by the petitioner challenging the validity of the detention was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order of the High court does not suffer from any infirmity. [ 10 31 E ] 2. The detention order is not vitiated by any error of law or fact. [ 11 43 B ] 3. The question whether the order is bad in law or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the order can be sustained on the sole ground that the detaining authorities did not apply their mind to the facts of the case, then the order cannot be quashed.

The appellant, a dealer in gold, was carrying on business as a money lender. He had been granted permission to carry on the business of gold and silver ornaments under the Gold Control Act, 1968. In the course of his business he carried on business in gold ornaments and other articles. The appellant's case was that the provisions of the Gold (Control) Act, 1969 were not applicable to him because the Gold Act did not provide for any restriction on the power of the Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer. The High Court held that the object of the Act was to protect the interests of the general public and therefore it was necessary to give an opportunity to the appellant to make his representation against the proposed action. It further held that there was no provision in the Act which required the Administrator either to grant a licence or refuse to grant such a licence. The order of the High Court was set aside by this Court. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned section was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it provided for the grant of a licence to a person who is intending to carry out the objects of the enactment and that the legislature could not be said to have intended to confer a right on a person to whom the Act applies to do so. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The object of enacting the Act is to prevent the evasion of tax. [ 10 56 B ] 2. The purpose of the legislation is to ensure that the Government does not act arbitrarily or capric iously in granting or refusing to grant the licence. [ 1057 E ] 3. The power conferred upon the Administrator under section 28 of the Customs Act is a very wide one and the discretion given to the Administrator must be exercised with due care and caution. The Legislature has made a distinction between the powers of the Collector and the powers conferred on him by sections 29 and 30 of the Sea Customs Act. [ 1060 A ] 4. Section 28 of Customs Act provides that the Administrator may grant a license or permit to a licensee or a person licensed under the Act to carry the goods specified therein. The word " license " is defined in section 2 (h) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The expression " license ", in section 28, means a license granted under the provisions Of the Act. The appellants were the trustees of a temple. They claimed to be the hereditary office holders and had been in possession of the properties for more than 25 years, and that they had been appointed as trustees by respondent No. 4. The trial court held that the appellants had failed to prove their title to the properties and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was wrong in holding that the plaintiffs had not proved their title and that the suit was barred under article 124 of the Limitation Act. Held: (1) that the question whether the alien or had been removed from the office of trustee is a mixed question of fact and law and cannot be decided in an application under section 100 C. P. C. [ 123 E ] (2) The burden of proof is on the person who asserts the right to the property and he must establish that he has acquired the title to it. If the person claiming adverse possession fails to prove his title, then the burden shifts to the person alleging it. But if he does not prove his possession, then it will be open to him to prove that he had acquired the right. The burden is on him to show that he did not have the right, but he has to show it. It is only when the person against whom the claim is made denies the title of the true owner that the onus shifts to him. The person who claims adverse possession must establish the same. The possession of a person who is entitled to a share in the property is not a mere co incidence. He is in possession and enjoyment of the property. [ 124 A B ] (3) The presumption of truth attached to the possession of one who claims to be in possession is not conclusive. The presumption is rebut table and the person asserting the possession must show that the possession is hostile to the real owner. The evidence adduced by the appellant shows that the respondents had no anim us to deny the title. The appellants'case is that the first respondent was in possession since the year 18 64 and that he was in actual possession of all the properties. The second respondent's case is based on the assumption that the appellant had been dispossessed by the first defendant after the death of the first plaintiff. The first respondent'S. R. T. N. Pillai, the first appellant, was the manager of the temple and the second respondent was the Manager of the Temple. The third respondent'was the Secretary of the deity. The fourth respondent'is the son of the second appellant. The fifth respondent'and the first respondents are the sons of the third respondent. The appellant's father died in 1933. The suit was filed in the year 1954. The respondents'case was that the idol was in the name of the appellant'and that there was a family arrangement between them. The idol was a Hindu festival and the idol and the temple were in the possession and management of the entire family. The temple was in existence at the time of the institution of the suit and the suit properties were in possession. The defendants'case that the temple was a public temple was not established by the appellants. The High Court held that there were no pleadings to the effect that the deity was in exclusive possession of any part of the land and that it was not a public place. On the other hand, the High court held the suit to be incompetent. The appeal was therefore allowed. The decree passed by the High. Court was set aside and the decree passed in favour of the respondents was confirmed. The State appealed to this court. HELD: The High court was right in its conclusion that the plaintiff's suit was not maintainable. The finding of the High, Court that the defendants were in adverse possession of that the property was not correct.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was granted a licence to run the Theatre in the year 1966. On July 22, 1966, the respondent No. 1 issued a notice to the appellant under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cin emato graph) Act, 1959, calling upon it to show cause why the licence should not be cancelled for violation of the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order passed by the District magistrate was without jurisdiction as the same was passed by an incompetent authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have power to issue writs under Article 226 of the Constitution against any order or decision of subordinate courts. [ 586 E ] (ii) The power conferred on the High Courts under article 226 is not intended to confer on them any right which is not expressly provided for in the Constitution. It is only when there is a specific provision in the statute conferring such power that the High court can exercise its jurisdiction under article 227 of the constitution. [ 587 G H; 588 A ] (iii) The powers conferred on a High Court under article 32 are wide enough to include within their sweep the power to quash proceedings taken under the Act. The power to make orders under the Code of Civil Procedure is not limited to the power of the High courts but extends to all other purposes including the power relating to the institution of suits and appeals. [ 589 B ] (iv) The word " proceeding " used in the context means " any suit or proceeding instituted before the commencement of the Ordinance ". The words " any proceeding " in the definition of " proceeding ", in the present case, do not mean a proceeding in the nature of a suit or other proceeding. The word'proceeding'in the first part of the definition does not necessarily mean a suit. The expression " proceeding in a court " in section 2 (c) of the Code has been defined in section 3 (d) of that Act. Section 3 (e) defines " proceeding ". The word is defined in the Act as meaning " any proceedings in a civil court including a proceeding under the Indian Penal Code." The word includes " in any other law for the time being in force " in clause (f) of section 2 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. The definition of the word " proceedings " in sections 2 (b), 2 (d), 2, 2 (e), 2. 2 (g) and 2 (h) of this Act makes it clear that the word'proceedings'in section 4 (1) of Act is not confined to the proceedings in the ordinary way of the criminal courts. The term " proceedings in any court " is not restricted to the ordinary course of the procedure prescribed by the Code. The words'proceedings in court'in clause 2 (a) of s. 2 of Act are not restricted by the definition in section 5 (2) of Code of Criminal Procedure. The Legislature has not included the word in the section. The use of the words " in respect of the proceedings " occurring in section 6 (1)( a) and the words'in respect thereof'in sub section (1). The word in section (2)( a), therefore, must be read as meaning the word, " in relation to the trial of the offence " in sub sections (1), (2), (3) and (4) of S. 2.

The appellants were granted a lease of the factory in respect of certain properties, and the respondent was given possession of the same. In pursuance of this agreement, the appellants entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale of the said property. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for a declaration that the appellants had no right to sell the said premises and that they were not liable to be evicted from the premises. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 12 of the Act as he had no authority to grant any such permission. Held: (1) that the provisions contained in section 12 are mandatory and do not affect the validity of the notice issued under section 12. Section 12 is only directory and does not affect any rights of the parties. It is true that the section does not expressly prohibit the exercise of the power of the Custodian or the State Government under section 10. But it is equally well settled that where there is a provision in a statute which gives a finality to the orders of the authorities, the same can be challenged in a writ petition. The words " any order passed by the Custodian " in section 10 (2) must be read as meaning the order of the Collector made under section 7 (3). The words'any order made by the Collector'in section 7 are wide enough to include a direction to the Custodian to dispose of the property in accordance with law. The expression " any person interested in the land " in s. 12 (1)( b) means a person who is interested in any land and includes a tenant. The word " any " in the context means a landlord or a tenant who has been allotted some land. The definition of the word " owner " in clause (c) of section 2 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, shows that the word'owner'is used in the sense of a person having a proprietary interest in the soil. The appellant was therefore entitled to the protection of section 18 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fr ag mentation) Act, 1948. The respondents were not entitled to claim the benefit of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court was wrong in holding that the proceedings before the Assistant Settlement Officer were without jurisdiction. The Assistant Settlement Commissioner was competent to decide whether the land was evacuee property or not. The decision of the Assistant Custodian was final and binding on the parties and the Assistant Commissioner was bound to give effect to the order. The question whether the Assistant Collector was competent under section 11 to issue a notice to the appellants did not arise because the Assistant Director of Consolidation was not a party to the proceedings. The Deputy Director of Estates was not competent to make the order under section 8 of the Administration of E vac uee Property Act, 1950. The appellants had not been able to show that the Assistant Consolidation Officer had jurisdiction to pass the order dated March 31, 1951. The order was therefore void and inoperative. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The judgment of the High court is set aside. The case will now be remitted to the Assistant. Settlement Officer for disposal according to law.

The appellant, who was a minor son of Raghubir Singh, filed an application under section 21 (1) of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 before the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanum angarh for determination of his ceiling area. He alleged that he had been in possession of the land and had not cultivated it. The Sub Divisional officer, Hanum angar, by his order dated 5th May, 1976 held that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and therefore, the provisions of the said Act were not applicable to him. The Board of Revenue, however, set aside the order of the Sub divisional Officer on the ground that the Sub Division Officer had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power of the Board of revenue could not be exercised by the Sub - Divisional Officer as the Sub division Officer had not passed any order under Section 221 of the Land Revenue Act. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power of superintendence conferred on the Board is wide enough to include all the powers which are necessary for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the statute. [ 728 E ] 2. The word'control'has been defined in section 2 (h) of The Rajasthan Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1975 which means " the right of resumption or re settlement ". It does not mean that the State Government can exercise its powers of superintendence over the Collector. The words'the Collector'have been used in the Act. The expression'the State'has not been defined either in the Rajasthan Land Revenue Code, 1959 or the Rajasthan Ten ants (Temporary Powers) Act. 1956. The definition of the word'State'in section 3 (c) of Rajasthan Act of 1957 is very wide and includes the State of Rajasthan. The Rajasthan Land Reforms and Res um ption of Jagir's Act, 1952, provides for the vesting of the estate of a tenant in the State. The State of Ajmer is also a part of the State and the State has the power to make rules for the management of the estates of the tenants. The Act of 1953 is a special law relating to the land revenue and the Rajasthan Im position of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973. The provisions of section 4 of the aforesaid Act of 1954 are not inconsistent with the provisions contained in the said Acts. The question whether the State Legislature had the power under the Rajasthan Act to enact the Rajasthan Abolition of Land Reforms Act, 1950, is a question of fact which cannot be decided by this Court.
