The appellant was a licensee and the respondent had been described as the licensee. He had also filed an application for eviction of the appellant from the premises in dispute on the ground that he was a tenant and not a licensee. The trial court held that the appellant was not a tenant but a licensee, and therefore, the appellant could not be evicted under section 14 (1)( b) of the Bombay Rent Act. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the trial court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the licence was granted to the respondent only for a period of five years and since the respondent did not vacate the premises within the said period, the licence could not have been terminated. It was further submitted that the respondent was a licence e and not the licensee and therefore the provisions of section 15 (2) of Bombay Rent Control Act were not applicable. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent was not entitled to any protection under the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947. [ 10 69 B ] 2. The question whether the respondent is a licensee or not has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 11 68 C ] 3. The object of the Act is to provide for the control of rents and repairs of certain buildings and for matters connected therewith. The Act provides for the regulation of the business of the landlord and the tenant and for the recovery of rent. Section 5 (4) of that Act provides that no suit shall lie in any Civil Court against the State Government or the Central Government for the eviction of any person who is in arrears of rent or damages for use and occupation of any building. [ 12 71 D ] 4. The word'occupier'used in section 2 (i) of Act means a person who occup ies the premises and includes a person whose name is entered in the register of tenants. [ 13 72 A ] 5. The definition of " occupier " in section 3 (c) of Maharashtra Act is very wide and does not include a person occupying a building or part thereof. The expression " owner " in the context of section 2 of the Maharashtra Act would mean a person holding over or in occupation of the premises. [ 14 E ] 6. The words " any person " in clause (a) of section 3 of the said Act are of wide import and must be construed in the light of the context in which they occur. [ 15 G ] 7. The term " occupier ", in section 4 (a), means a tenant or a sub tenant or an occupant. [ 16 F ] 8. The meaning of the word " occupier ". in section 5 (a)( i) is clear and unambiguous. There is nothing in the Act which requires the landlord to give notice to the tenant before letting out the premises to the landlord. [ 17 A ] 9. The language of section 5 is plain and unambiguous and there is no ambiguity in the language of the section.

The appellant, a resident of the former State of Rajasthan, was granted a permit for export of certain goods. The respondent applied to the Government of India for grant of a permit under section 3 of the Indian Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, on the ground that it had been granted in the interest of the general public and that the said order was not binding on him. The appellant contended that the agreement was void as it was not made by the Rul er of the erstwhile State of Jaipur but by the Central Government which was the successor State of the State of Ajmer. Held, that the contract was valid and enforceable and the appellant could not be allowed to claim refund of the amount paid by it to the respondent. The question whether the agreement is valid or not did not arise because the agreement itself was not a law. It was an agreement between the Rul ers of the two States and the latter State of Bombay. The agreement was not one of the States of Saurashtra and Kutch. The Domin ion of India was the only State in which the Rul ing of the United State of Saurashtra was concerned. The Rul er's right to import goods from outside the State was not affected by the provisions of article 286 (2) of the Constitution. The Union of India had no power to make any law imposing a tax on the sale of goods. There was no provision in the Constitution which authorised the President to make such a law and the President could not therefore make any such law. The terms of the agreement were not binding upon the Rul es of the other States. The agreements were not enforceable against the Rul e of the new State of Jodhpur. The contracts were not governed by the laws in force in the former States of Ajmer and the former Rajasthan. The rights of the Rul ors of the old States were protected by the Constitution and the rights of those who had entered into the agreement with the Rul or of the latter Rajasthan were not affected. The appellants were entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in article 286 of the Co ven ant. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed.

The appellants, who were the traders in cotton and ground nut, had been selling their goods to the purchasers. They sold them at a price higher than that fixed by the Government of Madras under section 5 (1) of the Act. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, as amended by the Madras Commercial Tax (Amendment) Act, 1953, which was later replaced by the Tamil Nadu General Sales tax (Amendment and Valid ation) Act. 1954. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the levy of sales tax on the sale of cotton and the purchase of cotton made by the appellants was not an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants'fundamental right to carry on business and that the impugned provisions were violative of article 19 (1)( g) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the provisions in the Act were discriminatory and violative of articles 14 and 19 (i) of constitution. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: (1). The object of the legislation is to prevent evasion of tax. It is not necessary that the legislature should have intended to make a provision for taxation. [ 93 B ] (2) The Legislature has power to make laws with respect to any matter within its legislative competence. The power to legislate is given to the executive and the legislature cannot delegate such power to another authority. If the legislature has no power to enact a law, the question of excessive delegation does not arise. [ 94 E ] (3) The power conferred on the executive by the Act is not un canal ised or un controlled but is subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution. The State can only impose restrictions on the exercise of the power. But the power is not absolute. The legislature can make laws imposing restrictions on certain matters. The restrictions are not arbitrary or unreasonable. The courts will not interfere with the discretion of the executive in the matter of granting exemption. [ 95 A C ] (4) The words " reasonable restriction " in the context of the present case must be read in the light of the object of legislation. The expression " reasonable " means " reasonable in the circumstances of the case ". The word " reasonable ", therefore, must mean " reasonable ". The words used in the statute must be construed in the sense in which they are understood in the trade and the object to be achieved by the statute. [ 96 G H; 97 A ] (5) The word'reasonable'in the definition of'reasonable in section 2 (d) of Act, means'reasonable '. The word is not defined in the Constitution and the word'includes'is generally used in relation to the word in the other statutes. The word may include'in some cases. The words'in all cases'are not sy non y mous with the words'the State'and'the Government'in other Acts. The meaning of the word is derived from the context in which the word has been used in these two sections. The first part of the section provides that the State shall not make any law which takes away or ab rid ges the rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution or any other law for the time being in force. The second part of section 2 of the impugned Act provides that nothing in the said Act shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse between the State and any other person or persons. The third proviso to section 2 provides that no such law shall be deemed to be invalid on the ground that it is inconsistent with any of the other provisions of this Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to this Court by special leave. The High Court held that the conviction of the appellant was not justified on the evidence of the eye witnesses, but on the ground that there were no independent eye witnesses to the occurrence and that the prosecution had failed to prove the motive for the crime. In appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court was in error in holding that the case against the appellant could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Held: (1) that the view taken by the High court is correct and that there was no reason to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. (2) that there are no circumstances which would justify the inference that the accused was guilty of murder or that he committed the murder. (3) that even if the High Courts have accepted the evidence as sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused, they must be given the benefit of doubt. (4) that in a case where the accused has been acquitted by the Sessions Judge, the High, Court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. (5) that when two views are possible, one pointing to the guilt and the other to the innocence of the person accused, the view which favour's the accused should be adopted. (6) that where the view of the High. Court is not reasonably possible, the judgment of the appellate court should be set aside.

The petitioner was a permanent Government servant and he had retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. He was compulsorily retired by order dated 3. 8. 1976. His services were terminated by an order dated 4. 9. 1976, which was served on him on 5. 11. 1976 and he was also compulsorily retired under Fundamental Rule 56 (j). The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of compulsory retirement made against him. The High Court dismissed his writ petition holding that the order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal was not sustainable in law as it did not have the effect of setting aside the order made against the petitioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the Central Government is not liable to be quashed because it has been passed without jurisdiction. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The power conferred upon the appropriate authority under Article 226 of the Constitution is wide enough to include within its ambit all executive actions including those taken by the Government or other authorities in exercise of statutory powers. It is not open to the court to read into the provisions of the statute words which are not there. If the legislature intended to give the same meaning to the expression " any other law for the time being in force " then the word'law'would have been used. [ 11 E F ] 3. The object of the Act is to provide for the regulation of recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. The purpose of the legislation is to make provision for the constitution of the State Public Service Commission for the appointment and conditions for the service of the persons appointed in the service. The Act provides for the establishment of the Commission and the functions of the Commissions are set out in Section 12 of the said Act. The Commission is a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal. It has its own constitution and is responsible for the administration of the affairs and business of the Government of India. The Government of the country is responsible to the people of India for the welfare of the people and for the protection of the interests of the citizens. The Constitution of India has given the wid est possible interpretation to the term'State'and the expression'State Government'in Article 12 of our Constitution means the President of India and the Governor of a state. The expression'person'in article 12 of its wid est sense includes the Government and the Legislature of the States and the local authorities. The word'State ', therefore, must be construed according to the dictionary meaning. The definition of'State in Article 366 (22) of the Indian Constitution is very wide and includes all the States in the Union Territories. The State of Jammu & Kashmir and the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir are two separate and distinct entities. The former is a part of the territory of India, while the latter is a Union Territory. The latter is governed by the Constitution. The second part of Article 12 is applicable to the State of Punjab and the third proviso to Article 309 of the constitution is not attracted. The first proviso to clause (1) of Article 311 makes the position clear. The proviso to the said clause (i) is not applicable to a case where the President is satisfied that the Government is the appropriate Government in the circumstances of the case. The words'in the case of a person'occurring in the second proviso to Clause (1), do not mean that the President can only be the Government. The President of the Governor is not the Governor in the State. It will be the Governor alone who is the appointing authority. The Governor is the head of the office. The Chief Minister of the concerned State is the Governor. The post of the Chief Minister is not created by the President.

The appellant Corporation was a public sector undertaking. It had taken a policy for the benefit of its employees and it was to be paid in accordance with the terms of the said policy. The respondent No. 1, who was the husband of the deceased, filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50, 000 / as full and final settlement of his claim. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree on appeal. In the second appeal by certificate, the High court held that the contract of insurance was concluded only when the premium was received by the Corporation and not before the death of the insured. The High Court also held that there was no concluded contract between the parties and therefore the question of payment of any amount did not arise. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Courts judgment is erroneous and should be set aside. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Courts have held that in view of the fact that the life assured died after the expiry of the period of the insurance policy, the contract was concluded and the Insurance Company was liable to pay the sum assured under the policy. [ 354 C ] (ii) The term " under writing " has been defined in section 2 (d) of the Insurance Act, 1938 which means an act or omission which is done in pursuance of a contract of indemnity. The word " under " is used in the sense of " under ". The word'under'is used to den ote the intention of the parties or their agents to give effect to the contract. The words " under the contract " are not sy non y mous with the expression " under written " and they are used in different's enses. The meaning of the word " Under " is " under ", " under," " under." [ 355 E ] (iii) The word under " in the context of the contract must be read as " under. " under, " is not a term of art. The contract of Insurance is one of utmost good faith and the word under stands the same. The purpose of the clause is to make the contract binding on the parties. The intention of both the parties is clear from the language employed in the clause. [ 356 G H; 357 A ] (iv) The words under lined in the first part of the definition of " Under writer " in section 3 (1)( c) of Insurance Act would mean under the definition given in the Insurance Policy, the risk of the Life Insurance Corporation being covered by the policy of insurance. [ 358 B ] (v) The true construction of the words " Under the contract ", in the light of the dictionary meaning of those words, is that the word'Under'is not meant to convey the meaning of " as per the contract between them " and the words under " under'are used to convey that the policy is a contract between two parties. If the contract is one for the purpose of giving effect to it, then the contract will be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act. [ 359 D ] (vi) The contract is not one of the kind mentioned in the definition clause. The term'under the Contract of Insurance'is to be construed according to the terms and conditions of the policy and the contract can be made applicable to the case of the insurer. [ 360 F ] (vii) The terms of contract of the present case are not identical with the contract in the instant case.

The appellants were the plaintiffs in a suit for recovery of money. They claimed that they had been in possession of certain properties as tenants and that they were entitled to receive rent from the defendants, and that the respondents were not liable to pay any rent. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled only to the amount of rent which was payable by them under the terms of the lease and that there was no question of their being in arrears of rent. In appeal the High Court held that since the appellants were not in arrears, the order of the High court could not be said to be final. It further held that even if it was assumed that the appellants had committed default in payment of rent, the decree would still be a final order and the High Courts should have directed the parties to maintain status quo till the disposal of the suit. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the High'Court was wrong in holding that the order passed by the High, Court was final and binding on the parties. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding in favour of the appellant that the application for stay of the execution proceedings was not maintainable. [ 704 E ] (2) The order of stay granted by the trial court was not final and the same was not subject to the result of the appeal. [ 705 B ] (3) The fact that the respondent No. 1 was in possession and enjoyment of the property is not disputed. The High court was therefore justified in directing the deposit of the amount. [ 706 C ] (4) The appellants are entitled to the benefit of the order dated April 30, 1968. [ 707 D ] (5) The appeal must fail.

The assessee company was manufacturing cotton fabrics and the process or was selling it to the process ors. The process or had been manufacturing the said fabrics in the course of its business, but the process was not carried on by the assessee. The assessee claimed that the value of the grey cloth should be taken as the assessable value of processed fabric and excise duty should be charged to the extent of the price at which the processed fabric was sold by the process of manufacture. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the assessee was entitled to a deduction of Rs. 20, 000 /- per month from the sale price of the processed fabrics. The Appellate Collector held that the assessable values were not the correct assessable value and directed the assessee to pay the differential amount of Rs, 20, 00, 000 /-. In appeal before this Court, the appellant contended that the decision of the High Court is erroneous inasmuch as the Tribunal has not given any finding on the question whether the assessee is entitled to the deduction of the value for the purpose of determining the assessable Value of the goods manufactured by it. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the process carried out by the appellant was a process or's manufacture. [ 345 B ] 2. The fact that the raw material was purchased by the manufacturer from the process / factory does not mean that the goods are manufactured by the processes or. The raw materials are sold by him. It is only when the raw materials have been used in the manufacture of the final product that the same can be considered as the raw - material. [ 346 C ] 3. The expression " in the process " in Rule 174 (1) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, means " in relation to the manufacture ". The word " manufacture " is defined in the explanation to Section 2 (f) of Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. The word'manufacture'is defined under section 2 (g) of that Act as meaning " bringing into existence a new substance known to the market ". The term " manufacture'includes any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. The definition of manufacture in the Central Excises & Salt Act is inclusive and not exhaustive. The words " in connection with the manufacture " do not include the processing of the finished article. [ 347 G H; 348 A ] 4. The test laid down in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs M / s. J. K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd., [ 1964 ] 6 S. C. R. 14, referred to. 5. The ratio of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the above case is fully applicable to the facts of the present case.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. He was promoted to the post of Head Clerk in January 1974 and he was confirmed in that post in course of time. On April 1, 1975, he was promoted as a Head Clerk. On March 14, 1975 he was reverted to his substantive post of head clerk. On May 15, 1975 the appellant was promoted by an order dated April 1. 1975. On February 21, 1975 a resolution was passed by the Government of Haryana for absorption of the appellant as a Clerk. In pursuance of this resolution, the appellant joined the service of the Panchayat on April 1 1975. The appellant's services were regularised with effect from April 1 1976. The State Government issued a notification under section 33 (2) of the Punjab Panchayat Samiti's and Zila Parishads Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) providing that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1 1973 shall be deemed to have been absorbed in the service or retired from the service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the panchayat Samiti until they are absorbed in Government service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to continue in the post after April 1 1972. It further held that the appointment of the respondent was not made by the appellant in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore, the termination of his services was bad. The appeal was preferred by special leave against the judgment of the High court. Allow ing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the State Government under section 34 (3) of Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 is wide enough to include all powers necessary for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the act. [ 737 B ] 2. The word " appointment " used in section 13 (4) of Act is not defined in the Act. It has been used in the sense of " appointment ". The expression " appointment ", however, does not mean appointment by way of promotion. The expression means appointment by direct recruitment or by transfer. The appointment is not a mere ad hoc appointment. It is merely a temporary appointment. The person who is appointed substantively to a post is not entitled to be considered for promotion. [ 738 E F ] 3. The words " appointment by promotion " in section 12 (4)( b) of that Act cannot be construed to mean appointment of a person by way direct recruitment. The term " appointment'in section 2 (g) of this Act includes appointment by transfer of a permanent servant. The definition of " employee " in Section 2 (h) of section 2 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, makes it clear that the word " employment " in the context would include appointment by a person temporarily appointed to a permanent post in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. [ 739 D ] 4. The fact that the petitioner was appointed temporarily to the office of a peon and was later transferred to another post in the same capacity does not make him a permanent employee. His appointment was purely temporary and could not be terminated without giving him any notice. [ 740 G H; 741 A ] 5. The contention that the right to be treated as a tenure appointment is a condition of service is not correct. The right to hold the post is a part of the status of a tenure holder. The tenure of the office is not one of tenure but is a tenure. The question whether the tenure is a term of tenure or not is a matter of policy. There is no doubt that the tenure of a government servant is not the same as that of a servant.

The appellant, who was the Mahant of a Math in the year 18 92, filed a suit for declaration that he had been the owner of the properties and that the income from the properties was his personal property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the properties were not the personal properties of the Mahant and that there was no evidence to show that the property was the personal property of the Math or the deity. It was further urged that the finding of the High, Court that the temple was a public one was erroneous because the temple itself was a private one and the temple had its own properties and the properties belonged to the Math and the deity was entitled to the benefit of the trust. Held: (1) that the question whether the properties are the personal or private properties of a Mahant is a matter which must be decided by the court on the evidence adduced before it and the High Courts have rightly held that the said properties belong to the temple and the idol is the absolute owner thereof. (2) that even if the temple is a public temple, the properties belonging to the math cannot be said to belong to it as the property of a religious denomination. (3) that in any event the properties of an individual do not belong to him. (4) that all the properties belong exclusively to the institution and the endowment is a private endowment created by the f ounder himself and therefore the properties devol ve on the deity and the institution has no right to the same. (5) that under section 7 of the U. P. Hindu Religious Endowments Act, the property vests in the deity only when the trustee takes possession of the property and the manager of the temple receives the money from the trustee. (6) that where the property is vested in a trustee, the trustee is bound to take charge of the same and to pay the same to the trustee; and the trustee has no control over the management of the affairs of the institution. (7) that since the property in dispute is a wa qf property, the trustees are entitled to recover possession of it from the person in whose name the property stands. (8) that there is no provision in the Act for the vesting of the management in the trustee of the deity in the temple. (9) that a mere direction to the manager to make arrangements for the management and administration of the endow ments of the Temple is not sufficient to clo the the trustee with the power to manage the affairs and administer the properties in accordance with law. (10) that if the property belongs to the deity, the manager can sue the deity for recovery of the amount due to the trust and the property vest in the manager. (11) that when the property vested in the trust, the Manager of the Trust is entitled to receive the money and the trust is liable to pay it to the person who is entitled thereto, the amount received by the trustee as the income of the endowment. (12) that it is not necessary to decide whether the property should be sold or given back to the trustees or the manager or the trustee, as the case may be, and the surplus, if any, should be paid to the persons who are entitled thereto. (13) that, in the absence of any such direction, the Commissioner of Wak fs should not proceed to recover the amount from the persons in possession of such property. (14) that no notice of the order passed by the Commissioner was necessary to be served upon the trustee and the Commissioner and the parties concerned were directed to appear before him at the time of hearing of the case.

The appellants were allotted certain lands in the village of Rai kot. They were allotted to the respondents on a rent of Rs. 10 per month and they were given possession of the land by the Custodian. The appellants filed an application for review of the order dated October 31, 1952, but that was dismissed on November 8, 1957. Thereafter, the appellants moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the orders passed by the Additional Custodian and the Deputy Custodian. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of section 19 (1) of the 1954 Act were not applicable to the case because the property had been acquired by the Government under the notification issued under section 12 (1). Held: (i) that the expression " any other law " in section 19 of the 1955 Act would include all laws which are inconsistent with the provisions contained in the Act and would be repugnant to the provisions thereof. (ii) that there is nothing in the language of section 18 (1)( b) of that Act which makes it clear that the said provision applies only to the State of Jammu & Kashmir and not to the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. (iii) that section 19 does not apply to the present case as the property in question was acquired by a private person and therefore the provisions Of section 19 do not apply. (iv) that in view of the fact that the property was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, the provisions relating to acquisition of the said property did not apply and the provisions regarding compensation could not be applied to the facts of the present cases. (v) that even if the property is acquired by private persons, the same cannot be treated as evacuee property. (vi) that since the property has been acquired under a valid allotment made in favour of the respondent, the property must be deemed to have vested in the Custodian under section 19. (vii) that no appeal lay against the order of the Custodian General or the Custodian, as the case may be, under section 20 of the Act. (viii) that under section 9 of the Administration of E vac uee Property Act, 1950, the Custodian has power to cancel the allotment of the property and to re allot it to any person who is entitled to receive compensation. (ix) that Section 19 (2) of this Act is inapplicable to the instant case inasmuch as the appellant's claim to the property being evacuee property was not taken into consideration at the time of the cancellation of the allotment. (x) that though the property belonged to the appellant, he was not entitled to the benefit of section 14 of the Punjab Security of Land Ten ures Act, 1953, and the rules framed thereunder. (xi) that as the properties were acquired by way of gift from the original owner, the appellant was not liable to pay compensation for the same. (xii) that on the date of the transfer of the properties, the right to receive the compensation was extinguished and the appellant became entitled to retain possession of those properties. (xiii) that after the transfer, the title to the properties was transferred to the Custodian and that the Custodian was not competent to take possession of these properties. HELD: (1.) (i). The words " any person " in the context of section 4 (1), namely, " any member of the joint family " in sub clause (i), means a person who holds the property as a co sharer or a coparcen er in the joint property. [ 271 B ] (ii). The word " any " in clause (1); and the words " a person " used in the definition of the word " person " clearly indicate that the person who has the right of ownership in the property of the deceased, and his heirs and legal representatives, is the person in whose name the property stands.

The State Public Service Commission, in exercise of its powers under Article 309 of the Constitution of India, issued a notification dated May 5, 1985 inviting applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspe ct ress of Girls Schools. In pursuance thereof, the State Government issued an advertisement on May 5 1985 inviting application from eligible persons for selection to the posts of Upper Primary School Teachers and Upper Primary Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women's Branch) The advertisement was published on May 4, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in the newspaper on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was held in two stages written and interview / personality test. After the written examination and interview were over, on the basis of the results thereof, merit list was prepared. On the basis thereof, a select list was published by the State Public Services Commission which was challenged before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State had no power to cancel the entire recruitment process and directed re holding of the recruitment afresh. The State Government filed an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of the State to cancel or withdraw the entire selection process is not limited only to the purpose of giving effect to the decision of the Selection Committee but also to the manner in which it has been done. [ 125 B ] 2. The object of making the selection process transparent and fair is to ensure that all eligible candidates are considered fairly and objectively. [ 126 C ] 3. The selection process must be fair and reasonable and should not be arbitrary. It is open to the State, if it so chooses, to pick out persons who are not eligible for selection and who have better chances of success. If any candidate is found un suitable for appointment, he may be appointed to the service. But where there are more than one person having the same merit, the selection would be made on the sole ground of merit. [ 127 D ] 4. The principle of equality as envisaged in Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution cannot be pressed into service in such cases. [ 128 E ] 5. The concept of equality is a positive concept. It has its own significance in certain circumstances. It cannot be applied in a vac u um. It can never be applied to situations where the State has an option to adopt a particular method of selection or make a choice between two altern atives. [ 129 G ] 6. The doctrine of equality in Article 14 is applicable only when the State acts in an arbitrary manner or failed to act reasonably. [ 130 F ] 7. The rule of law does not mean that the Government has the power to ignore the rules and devi ate from the rules. [ 131 H; 132 A ] 8. The question whether the State could cancel the selection and appoint a person to a post in the service after the selection has been made is a matter of policy. The Government has to decide what is best for the job and not for the Courts. [ 133 B ] 9. The fact that the selection was made on a wrong notion of the law or the procedure is not a ground for quashing the selection. [ 134 C ] 10. The mere fact that some of the selected candidates were given appointments in excess of the quota prescribed for them does not entitle the State for cancelling the entire selections. [ 135 F ] 11. The case of the appellants is covered by the decision in the case of Dr. M. S. Abdul Karim & Ors. vs State of Bihar & Ors., [ 1983 ] 2 SCC 141.

The appellant was the owner of a property in which he had an interest. He died on 13 10 1970 leaving behind him his widow, two sons and one daughter. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the property of the D era. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to be impleaded as a party under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court held that the appeal was incompetent because the appellant had no right to sue or to continue the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court should have allowed the appeal and remanded the case to the trial court for fresh disposal. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed by the High court is set aside and the matter remitted to the High. Court for fresh consideration. [ 489 B ] 2. The appellant has been given sufficient opportunity to defend himself before the trial Court. The appeal must be disposed of on merits. [ 490 C ] 3. The decree of the trial Judge is set side. The appellate court will decide the appeal on merits after hearing both sides. [ 491 E ] 4. The suit is pending since the year 1968. The parties are at liberty to file their pleadings and adduce evidence. [ 492 F ] 5. The plaintiff's suit is dismissed.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer in the year 1975 and were posted at the Head Quarters of the Board. In the year 1979, they were transferred to the Andhra State Electricity Corporation. On their transfer to the State of Andhra Pradesh, they had been working there for a period of more than five years. Their services were terminated by an order dated February 8, 1983. The petitioners challenged the said order before this Court in Writ Petition No. 45 71 of 1983. This Court dismissed the petition on the ground that it was not maintainable because the petitioners had no right to challenge the validity of the order passed by the Government. It is contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order was passed without giving any opportunity to them to show cause against the proposed action. Dismis sing the writ petitions, HELD: 1. The power conferred under Article 309 of the Constitution is wide enough to include within its ambit the power to make rules regulating the conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. [ 582 E ] 2. The proviso to rule 2 (b) of the Fundamental Rules which is a part of the Rule making power of the Governor is only enabling in the matter of prescribing the conditions subject to which the power may be exercised. The words " subject to the provisions of the Act " in the proviso are wide enough and do not confer any arbitrary power on the Government to alter the conditions attached to the service of the employees. [ 583 B C ] 3. The impugned orders are therefore invalid. [ 585 G ] 4. The contention that the amendment to the Fundamental Rule 2 (a) is ultra vires the powers of the Legislature is also devoid of substance. The amendment to Fundamental Rule is not a mere change of the conditions but is merely clarificatory in nature. [ 584 D ] 5. The amendments made to the Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1930, and the amendments thereto are not violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. [ 586 A ] 6. The amended rules are not inconsistent with the Constitution. The rules framed under the proviso to Article 309 are not in conflict with the provisions contained in the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder. [ 587 F ] 7. The High Court has rightly held that the amendments to the rules are valid. [ 588 H ] 8. The amending rules are in the nature of subordinate legislation and cannot be questioned on the grounds of violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 (1)( f) and 31 of the Con stitution. [ 589 A ] 9. The question whether the amendment of the rules is retrospective in operation does not arise since the amendment is not retrospective in character. [ 590 B ] 10. The effect of the amendment made in the Fundamental rules is that the rules and the amendment thereto are prospective in operation. [ 591 C ] 11. The object of the amending rules is to enable the Government servants to continue in service after the age of 55 years. The Government servant who has been appointed to the Service in accordance with the rules of recruitment and promotion, can claim seniority over the other members of the service. [ 592 B ] 12. The word'appointment'used in the context of the Rules is not capable of being construed in the same manner as the expression'appointment '. The word " appointment " means appointment to a permanent vacancy. The expression'temporary'is generally understood to mean a temporary appointment. The term'temporary appointment'is not defined in the Rules. The meaning of the word'temporary ', in the ordinary sense of the term, is not necessarily to be confined to temporary appointments.

The appellants are manufacturers of goods and they were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the Act. They filed returns for the assessment years in question on the basis that the raw materials purchased by them were not liable to tax under section 9 (1) of the C. S. T. Act, 1956. The assessing authority held that the purchases made by the assessees were not exig ible to tax as they had been sold by a dealer who was not a registered dealer within the meaning of section 2 (e) of C. P. & Ber ar Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appeals preferred by the assessee were dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In appeal before the Tribunal, it was contended that the purchase of raw material by the appellants was not liable for tax under Section 9 (l)( b) of Central Sales Tax, Act, 1948; that the sale of the raw material was not taxable under section 5 (3) of that Act because the raw - material purchased by the appellant was not sold by the dealers but by the purchasers; that there was no evidence to show that the appellants were selling the raw goods to the dealers; that even if the purchases were made by them, they would be deemed to have been exempted from payment of tax under s. 9 (I)( b); that the sales were not exempt from tax under cl. (c) of sub section (1), and therefore, the sales of the appellants could not be taxed under section 6 (1)( b). Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: 1. The purchase of the goods by the assesses is not an inter state sale or a sale in the course of export outside the territory of India. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The definition of'turnover'in section 2 of the Income Tax Act does not cover the transactions which are not covered by the definition of " turnover ". It is clear that the words " turnover " and " turnover ", in the context, do not mean the aggregate of the amounts received or receivable by the dealer. The expression " turnover'has been defined in section 4 (1). The word " turnover includes any amount received or payable by a person for the purpose of business or profession. The word'turnover ', in the present case, is not used in the sense of the term in the definition clause. The explanation to section 2 is only an inclusive one and not exhaustive. The words " in the case of sale " in section 5 of the Central Sales tax Act, read with the Explanation, indicate that the transaction must be of sale of goods. The sale of such goods is not a sale of those goods. Therefore, the sale is not exig ibility to tax. [ 11 E F ] 3. The fact that the goods are sold by dealers is immaterial. The goods are not sold in the State of Orissa. The sales are not in the ordinary course of business. The price paid by the purchaser is not the sole consideration for the sale. The seller is not liable. to pay the tax. The buyer is not entitled to claim deduction under section 7 (1 A) of Income Tax, 1961. [ 12 G H ] 4. The High Court was right in holding that the transactions in question were not sales. The question whether the sales in the instant case were sales in respect of which the assessee was not entitled under the Act, did not arise.

The appellant company was a dealer in cotton yarn. It purchased the goods from the seller and sold them to another person who was not registered dealer. The sales were made by the appellant to the buyers on their own account. The goods were delivered to the buyer at the time of the export. The appellant's contention that the goods had been despatched outside the State of Bombay is not correct. The sale was effected by the appellants to the purchasers at the destination where they were actually sent. The delivery of the goods to the purchaser was therefore, not an act of sale but a sale which took place within the State. The Sales Tax Officer held that the sales were not liable to tax under section 10 (b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. He also held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had any intention to evade payment of tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the words " a person " in section 10 of the Act did not mean a registered dealer as defined in section 2 (d) of that Act and that the word " a " in the definition of " dealer " in that Act could only mean a person who has given the declaration in respect of the sale of the commodity. HELD: (i) The expression " a registered person " used in section 8 (b), means a person whose name is entered in the register of dealers. [ 926 C ] (ii) The words " or a registered dealers " in sub section (b)( iii) of section 8 are wide enough to include a registered assessee. The words'a registered trader'in section 9 (b). do not refer to a registered manufacturer. They merely mean a dealer who sells the goods. The word " dealer ", in section 3 (c) of Act, means a registered or an unregistered dealer. [ 927 E ] (iii) The word'dealer'in the context in which the word is used in the section must be construed as having the meaning assigned to it in section 4 (b); and the word'a'in clause (c). [ 928 A ] (iv) The use of the word in section 5 (b): in section 6 (b)) does not make the word a dealer. There is nothing in the language of section 7 (b)- which would justify the conclusion that the legislature intended to give the word the meaning of the words'dealer '. [ 929 B ] (v) The High Court was right in holding that the expression " dealer'occurring in section 7 of the Madras General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1953, should be read as " a dealer ". [ 929 G ] (vi) The question whether the words in section 13 (b)] of the Central Sales Tax Acts of 1948 and 1956 should be interpreted in the light of the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and the rules framed thereunder, cannot be said to have been enacted with the object of making the Act applicable to the present case.

The appellant, a married woman, was living with her husband in the house of the respondent. She had been divorced by her husband and his wife. The respondent's husband had made an application to the Magistrate under section 125 (3) of the Criminal Procedure Code for maintenance. The Magistrate held that the respondent was not entitled to maintenance as she was not a divorce e. The High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate on the ground that the appellant was not the wife of the deceased. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the marriage between the parties was not proved. It was further urged that the evidence showed that the husband had no intention to marry the respondent and that he had never intended to marry her. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression " wife " used in section 127 (3)( b) is wide enough to include a wife who has been divorced from her husband. [ 78 E ] 2. Section 127 (1) provides that where any person has been lawfully married to another person and the other party to the marriage has not been lawfully wedded to the other spouse, such marriage shall be deemed to have been solemnized within the meaning of section 13 of the Act. [ 79 G ] 3. The word " wife ", in the context of section 127, means a person who has not only a wife but also a child. The term " wife'is defined in section 2 (f) of Act. The definition of " wife in section 3 (c) of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, which defines the expression " husband " in the following terms: " Wife " means a woman who is entitled to receive the maintenance of her husband or who is receiving the maintenance from her parents, and includes any person who is employed in a managerial or administrative capacity. [ 80 A B ] 4. The words " in relation to the person who may be entitled to the maintenance " in section 125 are very significant. They indicate that the legislature did not intend to make any distinction between the two classes of persons mentioned in section 126 (3). The expression'wife'in section 12 (1)( c) is not confined to the wife alone. The provision does not restrict the right of the wife to claim maintenance from the husband. The wife must be the wife, if she is able to maintain herself. If the husband is unable to maintain himself, the wife can seek maintenance from him. [ 81 C D ] 5. The object of the provision is to prevent vag ran cy and des titution. The provisions of section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not exhaustive of the subject matter of the dispute. The question whether the wife is entitled for maintenance from being the divorced wife or from her father is immaterial. [ 82 F ] 6. The fact that the wife has been living separately from her mother would not necessarily mean that she is entitled under section 127 of the code of Criminal procedure. [ 83 H; 84 A ] 7. The concept of the concept of " husband and wife " is not a new one. The law recogn ises the status of the husband as a separate entity. The relationship of the spouses is not merely a matter of contract. The husband is not liable to pay maintenance to the widow. The obligation to pay the maintenance is on the wife. [ 85 C ] 8. The amount of maintenance payable to the husband and the wife cannot be equated with the property of the joint family. The liability to pay a maintenance allowance is on account of the marriage. The right to maintenance is a statutory right. The payment of maintenance is dependent upon the income of the property. The quantum of maintenance depends upon the financial position of the person. The income of such property is not sufficient to meet the requirements of the family.

The appellant was a successful bidder in respect of the shop in question. He had bid for Rs. 11, 900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month. In pursuance of the order of the Collector, he deposited a sum of Rs. 1, 000 /- as earnest money and the balance amount was to be paid within one week from the date of receipt of the said order. On the same day, i. e., on 25. 3. 88, the appellant filed an application before the Collector stating that he had not been given any notice or opportunity of hearing and that he was not entitled to any relief. The Collector rejected his application by holding that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment. Hence this appeal. It is contended on behalf of the State Government that the order passed by the Collector is without jurisdiction because it is contrary to the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. It has also been submitted that the Collector has no power to pass any order under section 4 (2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. It was further contended that the appellant was not given any opportunity of being heard before black list ing him. It had been held by the High court that the rules do not express so. It would be open to the State to take such steps as are permissible under law. It could not have been done without following the principles of natural justice. It should have been held that the rule does not confer any right upon the appellant. The High Court did not consider the effect of the rules. It did not deal with the question whether the rules were mandatory or directory. It merely directed the Collector to give a personal hearing to the appellant and decide the matter afresh. The order of black listing was set aside. The State Government was directed to hear the appellant before passing the order. The appeal was accordingly disposed of. The respondents challenged the order in the High. Court. The Division Bench of the High, Court held that there is no requirement of giving notice before dis qualifying the appellant from participating in the auction. The learned Single Judge held that since the appellant had not made any representation against the order, the order was bad in law. The appellants'contention that the action of the authorities was illegal and void was rejected. The present appeal is directed against the decision of the Division Bench. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word " notice " used in Rule 9 (2)( b) of Bihar Land Revenue Code, 18 86 means " notice ". [ 10 42 B ] 2. The expression " notice ", occurring in Section 4 (1) of Act, makes it clear that the notice must be given either by the party to whom it is intended or by his agent or by registered post. If the person concerned is not served with the notice, the notice can be served by affixing it at some conspicuous place in the office of the authority. [ 10 43 C ] 3. The words " notice shall be given " in the proviso to sub section (2), of section 4 of the act, make it clear, that the person to whom the notice is given is required to be given a reasonable opportunity of making representation. [ 11 43 D ] 4. The object of the provision is to enable the person affected to know what is the nature of the interest in the property sought to be acquired. The purpose of the statute is to provide a speedy remedy to the person whose property is sought to acquire. The legislature has taken care to see that the persons interested in the land are not prejudiced.

The appellant, a tenant of the premises in question, was inducted as a tenant by the respondent on a monthly rent of Rs. 150 per month and he continued to pay the same till the year 1965. In the meantime, the respondent filed an application under section 10 (2)( vii) of the Bombay Rent Act for fixation of fair rent. The Rent Controller rejected the said application holding that the landlord had no right to fix the fair rent and directed the respondent to deposit the amount of rent with interest at 12 % p. a. from the date of the order. The High Court held that the respondent had not been able to show that there was any relationship between the parties and that the appellant was entitled to the protection of section 4 (1)( b) of that Act. It further held that since the respondent did not dispute the fact that the rent was fixed by the Rent Controller, it could not be said that the tenancy was created by him. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decision of the Rent Control Appellate Authority. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The object of the Act is to provide for the control of rents and eviction of tenants. The legislature has made a distinction between the two classes of landlords who are governed by the provisions of the [ Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act ] and the other class of landlords. The Legislature has clearly provided for the determination of the fair rents payable by the tenants to the landlord. The Act does not contemplate the determination by the Controller of the rent payable by a landlord or tenant. The landlord can only determine the fair rental value of the building and not the rent which is paid by the tenant to the owner. [ 550 B ] 2. Section 4 (3) of Act provides that where the landlord is a person who is liable to pay rent in respect of any building, the rent shall be determined by the standard rent which would be the fair market value of such building. [ 551 A ] 3. The expression " fair rent " used in section 4 of the Madras Rent Act means the rent actually paid or payable for the building. If the rent is not paid or is not payable in full, the landlord may recover the rent from the tenant. But if the rent paid is not the fair price of the property, the tenant will be entitled to claim the rent for the whole period of the tenancy. [ 552 C ] 4. The word " fair " in the context of section 5 (3)( i) of Madras Act, means the fair and equitable rent which the landlord might reasonably expect to receive from the owner of the land. The words " fair and reasonable " in section 5 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, indicate that the fair rate of rent is the rent that the tenant would have to pay for the entire building. The rent is calculated according to the standard rate of the standard rates prescribed by the Act. The standard rent is defined in section 2 (1) of this Act as the rent of the whole of the house let out to the tenant, but the rent charged by the landlord for the portion of the accommodation occupied by the owner, is the actual rent received by the occupier. The definition of the term'fair rent'in section 3 (1), therefore, is not exhaustive. The meaning of the word'fair'in the definition of'fair and'rent'is not in any way different from the ordinary meaning of'standard rent '. The word'rent ', in the present case, is a very wide connotation and includes the rent received from the landlord and the rent, which is the basis of the landlord's claim. [ 553 E; 554 F ] 5.

The petitioner, a senior citizen of the Indian Union, was given an opportunity to make a representation against the final list published. He made a representation on July 2, 1962, and the Central Government rejected it on August 1, 1963. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the final gradation list dated April 6, 1962. The High Court held that the final seniority list had been prepared without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to make his representation. It also held that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The principle of natural Justice is not applicable to administrative orders. [ 10 56 B ] (ii) The power of the Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution is wide enough to include within its sweep all administrative orders which are passed by the authorities subordinate to them. If the decision of the authorities concerned is mala fide or arrived at without application of mind, the same would be liable to be set aside. [ 11 56 C ] (iii) The order of the Central Administrative Tribunal is not vitiated by non consideration of relevant facts. [ 12 56 D ] (iv) The Central Government has not acted fairly and reasonably. The Central Administrative Tribunals have jurisdiction to entertain petitions for quashing the impugned orders. The petitioners have not shown sufficient cause for their failure to make out a case. [ 13 56 F ] (v) The question whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the matter is a mixed question of law and fact. [ 14 39 G ] (vi) The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to go into the merits of the case. The Tribunal cannot sit as a court of appeal over the decision taken by the appropriate authority.

The petitioners in the writ petitions are manufacturers of various items of goods. They have been granted Additional licences under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 and the said policy has been adopted by the Government of India for grant of import licences. In the case of the petitioners, the licence was issued under the Imports & Exports Policy 1978 80 which is applicable to the present case. The petitioners were granted Additional Lic ences under the said Policy. The licences were valid for a period of three years from the date of issue of the said licences. The petitioner's licence was renewed on the basis of the aforesaid policy. The respondents filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against the order of the Collector of Customs (Appeals) dated April 18, 1985. The Appellate Tribunal held that the petitioners had failed to make out a prima facie case for grant or refusal of the licence. It also held that there was no justification for granting the licence to the petitioners. The appeals preferred by the petitioners were dismissed by the Tribunal. Hence these appeals. Allow ing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 The petitioners have not made out a case for interference with the orders passed by the authorities below. [ 237 E ] 2. 1 In the instant case, the petitioners have been able to establish that they had imported the goods as per the Import Policy 1978 78 and the same were allowed to be cleared by the Customs Authorities. The goods were not cleared by them but were actually exported. The question whether the petitioners could be denied the benefit of the exemption notification does not arise. [ 238 G ] 2: 2. 2. The contention of the learned counsel for the petitioners that the goods should be assessed at the time of importation and not at the stage of clearance cannot be accepted. The fact that the importers had imported goods at the relevant time was not disputed. The only ground taken by the appellants was that the import was made after the expiry of the validity of the import policy. There is nothing on record to show that the imports were made after March 31, 1979. The import was effected on February 20, 1980. The imports were prior to the date when the import took place. The importers had not produced any evidence to show the import of the goods. The burden of proof was on the petitioners to prove that the imported goods were smuggled. [ 239 B ] 3. 1. The onus of proving that the importer had not discharged the burden of proving the existence of the circumstances relied upon by the Department is on the person who claims the goods to be liable to confiscation. [ 240 C ] 4. 2 The burden is on him to prove the existence and the nature of the burden cast on him. The department has not discharged this burden. [ 241 D ] 5. The High Court has rightly rejected the petitioners'claim that the burden was on them to prove their case. [ 242 F ] 6. 1 It is well settled law that the onus of establishing that the impugned goods are smuggled goods lies on the department. [ 245 A ] 7. 2 In the present cases, the burden is shifted to the department to prove its case. This burden is not discharged by the department but it is required to discharge the burden. The Department has not placed any material on record. The Commissioner has not given any finding on the point of the applicability of the doctrine of " preponderance of probability ". [ 244 H; 245 A, 247 C ] 8.

The appellant, a manufacturer of c offee and other goods manufactured by it, was selling the same in bulk to its customers. It had been supplying the said c offee to the buyers at the price fixed by the appellant. The appellant's factory was situated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The goods were sold in bulk and delivered to the customers at the factory gate. The containers were not returnable by the buyer to the appellant but were delivered to them at the destination. The delivery of the c offee was made on the basis of the invoice issued by the seller. The buyer was required to pay the price of the goods as per the terms of the contract. The price charged by the purchaser was inclusive of the cost of packing. The value of the packing material was included in the assessable value of such c offee. The Collector (Appeals) held that the cost incurred by the assessee was includible in the value of c uring the c uring of c ine. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the value should be determined under section 4 (4)( d)( i) of the Act and not under Section 4 (1)( b) of that Act. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The cost of c oking c offee is not includible in determining the value under section 4A (1) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944. [ 10 C ] 2. The question whether the cost has to be added to the price for determining the " value " of c oke o ven's does not arise in these cases because the cost is not included in determining " value ". [ 10 E ] 3. The words " cost of packaging " used in section 4 of the Central Excises and Salt Act are wide enough to cover the cost which is incurred by a manufacturer in respect of the excisable goods. The word " cost " is defined in section 2 (1), of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, which means the cost paid or payable to an assessee in respect thereof. [ 11 F ] 4. The expression " cost includes any amount received by way of excise duty or tax " in relation to the sale of c oc o an oil or c offee, etc., and includes the cost, if any, incurred by an assessee for the purpose of manufacturing the c oc oa. The definition of " cost ", in section 3 (1). of the Income Tax, 1961, shows that the expenditure must be incurred by him in respect to the manufacture of c ock ery. [ 12 G H; 13 A ] 5. The High Court was right in holding that the expenses incurred by way Of c offee cannot be included in computing the assessable income of the assessee. [ 13 B ] 6. The fact that the assessee had claimed deduction of the expenses from the price paid to the buyer of c akes, would not make any difference. The claim of the Revenue that the amounts spent by the respondent in respect o the c ock er es, c offee etc. were not includ able in the price, is not correct. [ 14 D ] 7. The Tribunal was right and justified in holding the cost ing of c ake and c offee as a part of the price. [ 15 E ] 8. The costs of c ree k, c ock ers, c oc ks, c akes and c akes are not liable to be included for the purposes of the computation of the assessable profits. [ 16 E ] 9. The respondent's contention that the price charged to the c oke is not includ in the cost and that the c ake is not a component of the value, is also not acceptable.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 161 I. P. C. and section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was tried by the Special Judge for the offences punishable under sections 161 and 165 I. PC. The prosecution examined PWs 1 to 3 as witnesses in support of its case. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 5 read with Section 5 (1)( d) of the Act and sentenced him to undergo R. I. for one year and a fine of Rs. 100. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to R. 1. The appellant has preferred this appeal by special leave. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of PW 1 is not reliable because he had not been examined by the prosecution. The evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is not corroborated by any independent witness. The recovery of currency notes from the appellant is not proved. The High Court did not accept the defence version that the currency notes were recovered from the possession of the accused. The presumption arising under section 4 (1) of Prevention of corruption Act is rebut table. The courts below have held that the appellant had failed to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction under section 7 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act is set aside. The appeal is allowed.

The petitioner was a director of the company and he was in charge of the affairs of the Company. He was also responsible for the day to day management of the business of the respondent company. In the course of his employment, he had been employed by the company as an officer or employee of the appellant company. On account of the fact that he was not in possession of any property, he was removed from service on the ground that he had no means of livelihood. The High Court held that the provisions contained in section 630 (1) were attracted only when there was a contract between the employer and the employee and that the termination of the employment was not justified under the terms of the contract. It further held that since the respondent was not a workman within the meaning of section 2 (s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the termination was illegal and void. The question whether the termination amounted to retrenchment was left open. The appellant's appeal before this Court was dismissed. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The words " any person " used in cl. (b) of sub section (1), are wide enough to include a person who is employed in connection with the affairs or business of a company. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The expression " any such person " in cl.( b) must be read in the context of the definition of " workman " in section 2. If the expression " workmen " is construed widely, it would mean a person employed in a managerial capacity and not in any other capacity. [ 11 E F ] 3. The word " workman ", in the first part of the section, has been used in the sense of a person whose name appears in the list of persons employed in the industry. The second part of clause (b), which deals with the definition, does not refer to a person, who is not a member of the establishment. The third part of cl. 2 (b)( i) refers to a workman who is a member or an employee of a factory or an industrial undertaking. The term " workman'is defined in section 4 (1). The definition of the word " worker " in the Act includes any person who has been employed in any industry to do any skilled or unskilled work for hire or reward. The definition is inclusive of all kinds of work which may be done by a person in the course or in relation to the business or occupation of the employer. The use of the words " in connection therewith " in clause (c) of section 1 of the Act makes the position clear. [ 12 G H; 13 A ] 4. The object of the legislature in enacting the law is to make the provision for the protection of the workers and the protection afforded by the Act to them. The purpose of the enactment is to provide a special procedure for the enforcement of the rights conferred by the statute. The Legislature has made the law for the benefit of the employees and the benefit thereof. The Act provides for the payment of gratuity to the employees. The scheme of the legislation is intended to provide for the welfare of the workmen and the right to receive gratuity. The employees have been given the status of a permanent employee. The benefits of gratuity and pension are provided for the employees of the State Government. The State Government has the power to make rules for the purpose of providing for the conditions of service of the officers and servants of the Government.

The appellant was a public trust. He had been managing the temple in his capacity as a trustee of the deity and he was also a member of the public. The temple was constructed by the trustees for the benefit of the devo tees. The appellant's father, who was an employee of the temple, was a member and was looking after the affairs of the Temple. The idol was installed in the temple on behalf of the appellant. The deity was not a private one but was a private temple. The worship pers were not only the servants of the f ounder but they were also the servants and agents of the Sansthan. The management of the property was taken over by the Government under section 18 (1) of the Act. The properties were held by the appellant as a public religious endowment. The High Court found that the temple was a Public Trust within the meaning of section 2 (13) of Act. It further held that the appellant was entitled to be registered as a Public trust under the Act and the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, were applicable to it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant is a public charitable trust within the definition of section 3 (14) of Bombay Public Trust Act, 1951. [ 531 E ] (ii) The word " public " has been defined in section 2 of the said Act to mean any person who is interested in the administration of the trust or its affairs and includes a manager, secretary, agent or other person acting in the ordinary course of business of the Trust. The expression " public trust " is wide enough to include a trust created for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the institution. The word'public'is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the sense of a legal term. The words " for the purposes of the present case " are not sy non y mous with the words " religious faith ". The word is used in section 4 (1)( b) of that Act which defines the expression " religious trust " as including a public temple. [ 532 A B ] (iii) The expression'religious trust'is defined in clause (d) of section 5 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 19 12, which provides that a public char ity shall be deemed to have been established by the f oun ders of the religious institution. [ 533 C ] (iv) The definition of the word'religious'in section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, does not refer to any particular form of religious belief or practice. The definition in section 5 (1), therefore, cannot be applied to the present context. [ 534 D ] (v) The words'religious worship'in the definition in the section must be given their natural meaning. The question whether a particular religious trust is a private or a public one is a matter of fact and is not a matter for the court to decide. [ 535 G ] (vi) The object of the ded ication of the idol is to provide for the performance of the worship of the de ities and the worship is a religious purpose. The ded ication is not to be made for the worship per but to the religious worship pers. The mere fact that the worship pers are the members of the family of the deceased, would not make the ded ic ations for the temple. There is no evidence that the deity was a religious institution or that the idol was a part of the religion. [ 536 F ] (vii) The idol is a place of worship and the idol of the God is a part and parcel of the entire family. The right of the members to worship at the temple is a right to worship the deity. The fact that there is a temple in the village and the deity is a member thereof is not in dispute. [ 537 H;

The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1943 44. The Income tax Officer, however, did not accept the certificate and proceeded to assess the appellant on the ground that the certificate had been issued by his predecessor in interest and that it was not open to the Income - tax Officer to make any addition or alteration in the certificate. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the exemption notification and that the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was correct. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have taken the view that the expression " other than the State " in section 13 (3) of that Act is wide enough to include all cases where the State has no power to impose a tax on the sale of goods. [ 890 C ] (ii) The word " State " used in section 4 (1) of Act is wider than the word " Government ". It is also clear that the word'Government'in section 3 (1)( b) means the Government of India. [ 891 B ] (iii) The words " the Central Government " in the context of section 4 of the Act are wide enough and do not mean the Government alone. The word'State'in the definition of the word in section 2 (c) of section 3 of the Indian Income tax act does not mean a State within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution. [ 892 E ] (iv) The expression " State Government " occurring in section 5 (1), therefore, must be construed in the light of the definition contained in section 6 (2). [ 892 A ] (v) The term " State ", in section 7 (1). of the Bombay General Clauses Act, 19 04, is wide and comprehensive enough to cover every kind of State action including those which are within the scope of the State Legislature. The expression'State ', in section 8 (1); and the expression'Union'in sub clause (a) of clause (1)' of section 2 of the General Clauses (1 & 2) thereof, clearly indicate that the State Government can make a declaration under section 3. The State Government may, if it so desires, make such declaration. But the State cannot make a law under section 4. The question whether the State can make such a declaration is a matter of policy and the court will not, therefore, be justified in making a declaration.

The management of the factory was taken over by the Central Government under section 3 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The employer has no right to withhold payment of the wages if he is required to do so. The provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, are applicable to the case of the workmen. The terms of employment of the workers are governed by the provisions of that Act.
