The appellant tenant was in occupation of the premises for a period of 10 years and he had been paying rent to the respondent. In the year 1976, the appellant filed an application under Section 20 (2) of the U. P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Let ting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the premises were let out to him by the landlord for a fixed term and that the suit was filed within the period of limitation as provided under sub section (1) of Section 20 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case to the trial court for deciding the question whether the suit is barred by limitation or not. The High Court held that since the suit has been filed beyond the period prescribed under the Act, it would be governed by the provisions of the said Act and therefore the suit should have been dismissed. It further held that the appellant tenant could not be evicted from the suit premises because the suit had been filed after expiry of the period. The appellant's appeal before this Court was also dismissed. In view of the fact that the matter was pending in the High Courts, the High court passed the order directing the parties to maintain status quo till the disposal of the suit. The appellants contended that the High courts below committed error in holding that the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of the provision contained in Section 20 read with Section 20 and the High C ount was not justified in dismissing the suit on the grounds mentioned in the judgment. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1. The expression " any person " used in Section 2 (e) of U. T. Act means a person who is liable to pay rent for any building or rented land. [ 161 E ] 1. 2. The word " person " in Section 3 (c) of Act includes a person whose name is entered in the record of rights or other particulars of the assessment list. [ 162 B ] 1 (a) The words " any other person " occurring in Section 4 (1)( b) of which the word " any " is used in the context of the definition of the word'occupier'in Section 5 (1). The word'owner'in the definition clause is defined in Section 6 (1), which reads as follows: " owner " means the person who, for the time being, is in possession or has control over the property and includes a mortgagee in possession, a person in actual possession, and a tenant of such a person." [ 162 G H; 163 A ] 2. 1 The word owner in Section 21 (1)) does not mean the person in possession of the property. The words'any person'in section 2 (1 - A) are only des cri ptive of the person and not the owner. The legislature has clearly intended that the word owner must include a person having possession of a building. The Legislature has not included a person as a person without title. [ 164 D ] 2 (a). The words used in section 21 (i) are " any building ". The word used in this section is " any premises ". The words in section 20 (1): " any land or building or part thereof, in respect of which a declaration has been made under section 3, shall be deemed to be a building if the land or part of the building is used for a purpose other than that for which it was leased, or for the purposes of which it is let out, and it is immaterial that the building or the part is used only for the purpose of the lease. [ 165 F ] 2.

The appellant was a th ika tenant in respect of the premises in question. He had been paying rent to the landlord for the period from 1. 4. 1949 to 31. 3. 1953. On the date of the commencement of the Act, he was a tenant under the respondent and his tenancy was terminated by notice dated 18. 6. 1954. The appellant filed an application before the Subordinate Judge for ejectment on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation as the respondent was not a th ata tenant within the meaning of section 2 (b) of the Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy Act, 1949. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 3 of the said Act because the respondent had not made any claim to the land in dispute. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that section 3 did not apply to the facts of the case. Held, that the expression " th ika tenants " used in section 3 must be given its ordinary meaning and that the word " th ata " in section 2 of the Bengal Thi ka Rent Control Act, 1947, means " a person who is liable to pay rent for any premises ". The word " tenant " in the context of section 5 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act is wide enough to include a person whose right to occupy the premises has been taken away by the provisions of the statute. The words " th ati t " in sub section (1) of section 4 of the aforesaid Act are wide enough and they do not mean that the legislature intended to exclude the tenants from the protection afforded by the Act. The word'th ika'in section 4 (1)( a) of that Act is not defined in the Act but is a word of wide import. It is well settled that the Legislature can make a law relating to the subject matter of the enactment only if the language of the provision is plain and unambiguous. The Legislature cannot be presumed to have intended to confer a power on the Legislature to make a particular provision of the law which would be repugnant to the provisions contained in the other sections of the same Act.

The High Court of Allahabad has held that the pay scale of Bench Secretaries Grade I with effect from January 1, 1986 was not discriminatory and that the same was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the classification made by the State Government is arbitrary and unreasonable. It was also urged that the decision of the High court was based on a wrong interpretation of the Rules and that there was no justification for the High Courts to have interfered with the said decision. Allow ing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts are entitled to take into account the fact that the Chief Justice of the Court had granted higher pay scales than the one which he was drawing before the amendment of the rules. [ 303 E ] 2. The principle underlying the rule of equal pay for equal work is that the difference between the two classes of posts should be such as would bring about an intelligible differentia between those who are similarly situated and those who do not. This principle is applicable only when there is a clear discrimination between the persons who are differently situated. [ 304 B ] 3. The classification made under the Rules is reasonable and does not suffer from any vice of arbitrariness. [ 305 C ] 4. The concept of equality before law demands that all persons similarly circumstan ced shall be treated alike both in privileges conferred and liabilities imposed. There is no warrant for the submission that there must be a reasonable classification. [ 306 F ] 5. The doctrine of classification is founded on the principle that " Equal Pay for Equal Work " means that all those who perform identical duties and responsibilities and those that are comparable are entitled equally to the same treatment. [ 309 A ] 6. The distinction between the nature of work and the degree of responsibility is a matter of degree and the nature and quality of work performed by the employees. [ 308 G ] 7. The nature of duties and functions discharged by the members of the subordinate judiciary and the need for the same cannot be ignored. [ 310 D ] 8. The power of judicial review in matters relating to pay scales or emoluments is limited. The Court can interfere with the decision taken by the executive authorities in exercise of their powers of judicial Review. [ 311 H; 312 A ] 9. The scope of judicial scrutiny in respect of the order of the Executive and the Governor is limited and the Court cannot substitute its own judgment for the judgment of the executive. [ 313 C ] 10. The expression'equal pay'implies the idea of something more than what is necessary for the purpose of the decision. [ 314 B ] 11. The word'equal'used in Article 14 is of the wid est possible amplitude and it covers cases of persons who have been differently situated and have been given the same status. The words'equal in rank'or'similar'in Article 16 (1) are wide enough to include within them not only those who have got the same pay but also those who were in service. [ 315 B ] 12. The object of the rule is to give equal pay to the persons appointed to the post in the same cadre. The rule of equality of opportunity in the matter of employment is a face t of equality. The right to equality is a part of the basic structure of the constitution. The Constitution has provided for equality of status and the dignity of the individual. The protection of equal salary and equal opportunity in matters of public employment is not intended to be a fundamental right. The guarantee of equality is the guarantee against discrimination. The State has the power to make classification in the context of the interest of the person who may be employed. [ 316 E ] 13. The question whether the classification is reasonable or not depends upon the nature, the source of the power.

The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. It had a registered office in the State of Madhya Pradesh and it was registered as a Company under the Indian Companies Act. The appellant companies were incorporated under section 3 (1) of the Act. Under the provisions of the said Act, the Central Government was empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Central Act. Section 2 (e) defines " local authority " to mean any municipal corporation or municipality or other local authority constituted by or under any law for the time being in force. Section 3 (f) defines'local authority '. Section 4 provides that the State Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare that the local area in which the Corporation is established shall be deemed to be a local authority for the purpose of this Act. By virtue of the aforesaid provision, the State Legislature has been empowered to enact the impugned law. The High Court held that the impugned legislation was within the competence of the State legislature. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power of the Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution was not subject to the legislative competence of Parliament. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power of Parliament to enact a law relating to a particular subject is a legislative power. [ 10 31 B ] 2. The expression " local area " is defined in section 2 (d) of Act No. 21 of 1951. The word " local " is not defined in the Act but it is used in the sense of " local areas ". The expression means the area within the limits of a Municipal Corporation or a Municipal Council or a Nagar Panchayat or a Cantonment Board. The words " Municipal Corporation " are wide enough to include a Municipal Committee, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation, Municipal Board, Municipal Committee etc. [ 11 E F ] 3. The Act is a piece of legislation enacted by the State Legislatures. The Union Territories Act, 1963, is an enactment passed by the Legislative Assembly of the States. The powers of the Union and the State Governments to make laws are contained in Entry 24 of List II of the 7th Schedule to that Act. [ 12 G H; 13 A ] 4. The entry relating to " Municipal Councils " in the Seventh schedule to the Act is not confined to the State. The entries in the three Lists of the seventh Schedule to it are not restricted to the Union territories. The two Entries in the third Schedule to Article 246 (1), namely, " Municipal Corporations ", " Municipal Committees " and " Municipal Boards " are not included in the list of the Concurrent Legislative Lists. The second part deals with the " Municipal Authorities " in respect of the " Municipalities " and its " the Union " in regard to the Corporation of Delhi. The third part of item (i) of sub clause (ii) of clause (b) of article 243 Q is not applicable to the Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils and Municipal Boards. The fourth part of article 246 (2) of Constitution of India is not attracted to the present case. [ 14 C ] 5.
